through sin, by involvement in its condition of
corruption and decay. See also ARIANISM. A.E.L.
atheism (from Greek a-, ‘not’, and theos, ‘god’),
the view that there are no gods. A widely used
sense denotes merely not believing in god and is
consistent with agnosticism. A stricter sense
denotes a belief that there is no god; this use
has become standard. In the Apology Socrates is
accused of atheism for not believing in the ofﬁcial
Athenian gods. Some distinguish between theo-
retical atheism and practical atheism. A theoretical
atheist self-consciously denies the existence of a
supreme being, whereas a practical atheist may
believe that a supreme being exists but lives as
though there were no god.

A¯ tman, in Hindu thought, the individual, viewed
by Advaita Vedanta as numerically identical to,
and by other varieties of Vedanta as dependent on
and capable of worship of, Brahman. Sometimes
in Hinduism conceived as inherently conscious
and possessed of intrinsic mental qualities, and
sometimes viewed as having mental qualities
only in the sense that the composite of A¯tman-
embodied-in-a-physical-body has this feature, A¯tman
beginninglessly transmigrates from life to life
(or, for Advaita, appears to do so). It is embodied
in successive bodies, accumulating karma and
possibly achieving enlightenment with its conse-
quent release from samsa¯ra, the transmigratory
wheel.

atomism, ancient. See ANCIENT ATOMISM.
atomism, logical. See RUSSELL.

atonement, the state of being at one or recon-
ciled; in its main sense, the means by which such
reconciliation is achieved and, more speciﬁcally,
the sacriﬁcial act by which such reconciliation is
achieved. All this implies that the parties to be
reconciled are initially estranged from each
other.
Some Christian theologians think Christ’s sac-
riﬁce includes his life, but most think it especially
involves his suffering and death. In Christian
theology, our sin estranges us from God, and
Christ’s sacriﬁce is a necessary part of a sufﬁcient
condition that cancels such sin. There are, how-
ever, different theories as to how Christ’s sacriﬁce
does this. Historically, there are at least three
main theories. The ransom theory says that our
sin enslaves us to the Devil, and Christ’s sacriﬁce
ransoms us from slavery. The satisfaction theory,
associated with Anselm, says that our sin incurs a
debt to God, and Christ, by his sacriﬁce, compen-
sates God, in our place, for the debt. The penal
substitution theory says that, on account of our sin,
we deserve to be punished, and Christ, by his
sacriﬁce, is punished in our place. These theories
are not exclusive, and one may combine some
or all of them.
See also ANSELM, GRACE, PUNISHMENT, SIN.

attribute. See PROPERTY.
attribution theory, a theory in social psychol-
ogy concerned with how and why ordinary peo-
ple explain events. People explain by attributing
causal powers to certain events rather than
others. The theory attempts to describe and
clarify everyday commonsense explanation, to
identify criteria of explanatory success presup-
posed by common sense, and to compare and
contrast commonsense explanation with scien-
tiﬁc explanation. The heart of attribution theory
is the thesis that people tend to attribute causal
power to factors personally important to them,
which they believe covary with alleged effects.
For example, a woman may designate sexual
discrimination as the cause of her not being
atheism
attribution theory
68
promoted in a corporation. Being female is
important to her and she believes that promotion
and failure covary with gender. Males get pro-
moted; females don’t. Causal attributions tend
to preserve self-esteem, reduce cognitive disso-
nance, and diminish the attributor’s personal
responsibility for misdeeds. When attributional
styles or habits contribute to emotional ill-being,
e.g. to chronic, inappropriate feelings of depression
or guilt, attribution theory offers the following
therapeutic recommendation: change attributions
so as to reduce emotional ill-being and increase
well-being. Hence if the woman blames herself
for the failure, and if self-blame is part of her
depressive attributional style, she would be
encouraged to look outside herself, perhaps to
sexual discrimination, for the explanation. See
also
EXPLANATION,
MOTIVATIONAL
EXPLANA-
TION.
G.A.G.
attributive pluralism. See PLURALISM.
attributive use of descriptions. See THEORY OF
DESCRIPTIONS.
Audi, Robert (b.1941), American philosopher
known for a comprehensive theory of reasons
and rationality, an epistemologically sophisti-
cated intuitionist theory in ethics, a liberal theory
of the relation between religion and politics, and
distinctive accounts of belief, desire, intention,
and practical reasoning. An overarching aim of
much of his work is to defend a non-skeptical
theory of rationality and to account for how
theoretical and practical rationality combine in
determining the overall rationality of a person –
“global rationality” (The Architecture of Reason,
2001). In epistemology, Audi combines internal-
ism about justiﬁcation with externalism about
knowledge, both justiﬁcation and knowledge
being structurally foundational. He considers
the basic sources of justiﬁcation broadly experien-
tial, but in a way that accommodates a priori
knowledge, for which he takes self-evidence
as
basic
(The
Structure
of
Justiﬁcation,
1993;
Epistemology, 3d ed. 2010). Audi extends his
epistemological theory to philosophy of religion,
particularly the relation between reason and faith
(Rationality and Religious Commitment, 2011); social
epistemology, centering on a theory of testimony;
and ethics, with moral epistemology as a major
element.
Audi is highly prominent in the revival of
ethical intuitionism understood as including an
account of moral knowledge and a pluralist moral
theory of the sort defended by Ross. But Audi has
developed the view far beyond Ross and the
classical intuitionists. Audi’s moral epistemology
combines an account of a priori knowledge of
moral principles with a theory of moral percep-
tion that addresses the possibility of knowledge of
particular moral facts such as the injustice of spe-
ciﬁc acts (Moral Knowledge and Ethical Character,
1997; Moral Perception, 2013). His normative
moral theory, like Ross’s, features a plurality of
principles of prima facie duty, although, unlike
Ross, Audi argues that such principles, though
self-evident and knowable a priori, can be ratio-
nalized by a liberal interpretation he offers of the
humanity formula of Kant’s categorical impera-
tive. The result is a uniﬁed Kantian intuitionism
that avoids charges of dogmatism and arbitrari-
ness often leveled against older versions of intui-
tionism (The Good in the Right, 2004).
In philosophy of mind and action, Audi has
developed accounts of acting for reasons, free-
dom and compulsion, self-deception, weakness
of will, and related notions. Each account is
guided by the conviction that plausible views of
these should be psychologically realistic in posit-
ing mental states and processes, in order to
avoid, for instance, over-ascription of inferences
and propositional attitudes in explicating justiﬁ-
cation, knowledge, and rational action (Action,
Intention, and Reason, 1993).
See also
ACTION
THEORY,
EPISTEMOLOGY,
ETHICS,
INTUITION,
JUSTIFICATION,
PRACTICAL
REASONING, ROSS, SELF-EVIDENCE.
M.C.T.
Augustine, Saint, known as Augustine of Hippo
(354–430), Christian philosopher, church father,
and one of the chief sources of Christian thought
in the West. His importance for medieval and
modern European philosophy is impossible to
describe brieﬂy. Matters are made more difﬁcult
because Augustine wrote voluminously and
dialectically as a Christian theologian, treating
philosophical topics for the most part only as
they were helpful to theology – or as corrected
by it. He fashioned the narrative of the Confessions
(397–400) out of the events of the ﬁrst half of his
life. He thus supplied later biographers with both
a seductive selection of biographical detail and a
compelling story of his successive conversions
from adolescent sensuality, to the image-laden
religion of the Manichaeans, to a version of
Neoplatonism, and then to Christianity. The story
is an unexcelled introduction to Augustine’s
views of philosophy. It shows, for instance, that
Augustine received very little formal education
in philosophy. He was trained as a rhetorician,
and the only philosophical work that he mentions
attributive pluralism
Augustine
69
among
his
early
reading
is
Cicero’s
(lost)
Hortensius, an exercise in persuasion to the study
of philosophy. Again, the narrative makes plain
that Augustine ﬁnally rejected Manichaeanism
because he came to see it as bad philosophy: a
set of sophistical fantasies without rational coher-
ence or explanatory force. More importantly,
Augustine’s ﬁnal conversion to Christianity was
prepared by his reading in “certain books of the
Platonists” (Confessions 7.9.13). These Latin trans-
lations, which seem to have been anthologies
or
manuals
of
philosophic
teaching,
taught
Augustine a form of Neoplatonism that enabled
him to conceive of a cosmic hierarchy descending
from an immaterial, eternal, and intelligible God.
On Augustine’s judgment, philosophy could do no
more than that; it could not give him the power to
order his own life so as to live happily and in a
stable relation with the now-discovered God. Yet
in his ﬁrst years as a Christian, Augustine took
time to write a number of works in philosophical
genres. Best known among them are a refutation
of Academic Skepticism (Contra academicos, 386),
a theodicy (De ordine, 386), and a dialogue on the
place of human choice within the providentially
ordered hierarchy created by God (De libero arbi-
trio, 388/391–95).
Within
the
decade
of
his
conversion,
Augustine was drafted into the priesthood (391)
and then consecrated bishop (395). The thirty-
ﬁve years of his life after that consecration were
consumed by labors on behalf of the church in
northern Africa and through the Latin-speaking
portions of the increasingly fragmented empire.
Most of Augustine’s episcopal writing was polem-
ical both in origin and in form; he composed
against authors or movements he judged hereti-
cal, especially the Donatists and Pelagians. But
Augustine’s sense of his authorship also led him
to write works of fundamental theology conceived
on a grand scale. The most famous of these works,
beyond the Confessions, are On the Trinity (399–412,
420), On Genesis According to the Letter (401–15),
and On the City of God (413–26). On the Trinity
elaborates in subtle detail the distinguishable
“traces” of Father, Son, and Spirit in the created
world and particularly in the human soul’s triad
of memory, intellect, and will. The commentary
on Genesis 1–3, which is meant to be much more
than a “literal” commentary in the modern sense,
treats many topics in philosophical psychology
and anthropology. It also teaches such cosmolog-
ical doctrines as the “seed-reasons” (rationes semi-
nales) by which creatures are given intelligible
form. The City of God begins with a critique of
the bankruptcy of pagan civic religion and its
attendant philosophies, but it ends with the depic-
tion of human history as a combat between forces
of self-love, conceived as a diabolic city of earth,
and the graced love of God, which founds that
heavenly city within which alone
peace is
possible.
A number of other, discrete doctrines have
been attached to Augustine, usually without the
dialectical nuances he would have considered
indispensable. One such doctrine concerns divine
“illumination” of the human intellect – i.e., some
active intervention by God in ordinary processes
of human understanding. Another doctrine typ-
ically attributed to Augustine is the inability of
the human will to do morally good actions with-
out grace. A more authentically Augustinian
teaching is that introspection or inwardness is
the way of discovering the created hierarchies
by which to ascend to God. Another authentic
teaching would be that time, which is a distension
of the divine “now,” serves as the medium or
narrative structure for the creation’s return to
God. But no list of doctrines or positions, how-
ever authentic or inauthentic, can serve as a
faithful representation of Augustine’s thought,
which gives itself only through the carefully
wrought rhetorical forms of his texts.
See also NEOPLATONISM, PATRISTIC AUTHORS,
PHILOSOPHY OF RELIGION.
M.D.J.
Aurelius, Marcus. See MARCUS AURELIUS, STOICISM.
Austin, John (1790–1859), English legal philos-
opher known especially for his command theory
of law. His career as a lawyer was unsuccessful
but his reputation as a scholar was such that on
the founding of University College, London, he
was offered the chair of jurisprudence. In 1832 he
published the ﬁrst ten of his lectures, compressed
into six as The Province of Jurisprudence Determined.
Although he published a few papers, and his
somewhat fragmentary Lectures on Jurisprudence
(1863) was published posthumously, it is on
the Province that his reputation rests. He and
Bentham (his friend, London neighbor, and
fellow utilitarian) were the foremost English
legal philosophers of their time, and their inﬂu-
ence on the course of legal philosophy endures.
Austin held that the ﬁrst task of legal philoso-
phy, one to which he bent most of his energy,
is to make clear what laws are, and if possible
to explain why they are what they are: their
rationale. Until those matters are clear, legislative
proposals and legal arguments can never be clear,
since irrelevant considerations will inevitably
creep in. The proper place for moral or theological
Aurelius, Marcus
Austin, John
70
considerations is in discussion of what the positive
law ought to be, not of what it is. Theological
considerations reduce to moral ones, since God
can be assumed to be a good utilitarian. It is
positive laws, “that is to say the laws which are
simply and strictly so called, . . . which form the
appropriate matter of general and particular juris-
prudence.” They must also be distinguished from
“laws metaphorical or ﬁgurative.”
A law in its most general sense is “a rule laid down
for the guidance of an intelligent being by an
intelligent being having power over him.” It is a
command, however phrased. It is the commands
of men to men, of political superiors, that form
the body of positive law. General or comparative
jurisprudence, the source of the rationale, if any,
of particular laws, is possible because there are
commands nearly universal that may be attrib-
uted to God or Nature, but they become positive
law only when laid down by a ruler. The general
model of an Austinian analytic jurisprudence
built upon a framework of deﬁnitions has been
widely followed, but cogent objections, especially
by Hart, have undermined the command theory
of law.
See also
JURISPRUDENCE,
PHILOSOPHY
OF
LAW.
E.L.P.
Austin, J(ohn) L(angshaw) (1911–60), English
philosopher, a leading exponent of postwar
“linguistic” philosophy. Educated primarily as a
classicist at Shrewsbury and Balliol College, Ox-
ford, he taught philosophy at Magdalen College.
During World War II he served at a high level
in military intelligence, which earned him the
O.B.E., Croix de Guerre, and Legion of Merit.
In 1952 he became White’s Professor of Moral
Philosophy at Oxford, and in 1955 and 1958
he held visiting appointments at Harvard and
Berkeley, respectively. In his relatively brief ca-
reer, Austin published only a few invited pa-
pers; his inﬂuence was exerted mainly through
discussion with his colleagues, whom he domi-
nated more by critical intelligence than by any
preconceived view of what philosophy should be.
Unlike some others, Austin did not believe that
philosophical problems all arise out of aberrations
from “ordinary language,” nor did he necessarily
ﬁnd solutions there; he dwelled, rather, on the
authority of the vernacular as a source of nice and
pregnant distinctions, and held that it deserves
much closer attention than it commonly receives
from philosophers. It is useless, he thought, to
pontiﬁcate at large about knowledge, reality,
or existence, e.g., without ﬁrst examining in
detail how, and when, the words ‘know’, ‘real’,
and ‘exist’ are employed in daily life. In Sense and
Sensibilia (1962; compiled from lecture notes),
the sense-datum theory comes under withering
ﬁre for its failings in this respect. Austin also
provoked
controversy
with
his
well-known
distinction between “performative” and “consta-
tive” utterances (‘I promise’ makes a promise,
whereas ‘he promised’ merely reports one); he
later recast this as a threefold differentiation
of locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary
“forces” in utterance, corresponding (roughly)
to the meaning, intention, and consequences of
saying a thing, in one context or another. Though
never very stable or fully worked out, these ideas
have since found a place in the still-evolving
study of speech acts.
See also ORDINARY LANGUAGE PHILOSOPHY,
SPEECH ACT THEORY.
P.He.
Australasian philosophy, the philosophical
work produced mainly by Australian and New
Zealand philosophers largely since World War
II. Australasian philosophy has been known
especially for its blend of analytical empiricism,
logic, and realism – applied uncompromisingly
to central questions in metaphysics, ethics, epis-
temology, philosophy of science, philosophy of
mind, and more.
For example, in
the 1950s, U.
T. Place
(“Is Consciousness a Brain Process?” 1956) and
J. J. C. Smart (“Sensations and Brain Processes,”
1959) identiﬁed the mental with the physical.
The result is still called “Australian materialism.”
D. M. Armstrong (A Materialist Theory of the Mind,
1968) built upon that base. Australian philoso-
phy has challenged that materialism, too. Frank
Jackson (“Epiphenomenal Qualia,” 1982) asked
whether one could know everything physical
about color without having whatever knowledge
arises from experiencing color. David Chalmers
(The Conscious Mind, 1996) confronted material-
ism with the conceivability of zombies – physical
beings functionally equivalent to human beings
but lacking consciousness. Functionalism – a
target of Chalmers’s criticism – has been repre-
sented by David Braddon-Mitchell and Jackson
(Philosophy of Mind and Cognition, 1996/2007);
and consciousness is receiving much attention
from
Australian
philosophers,
for
instance
Chalmers (The Character of Consciousness, 2010)
and Daniel Stoljar (Ignorance and Imagination,
2006).
In addition to that concern with mental prop-
erties, Australian philosophers have discussed
properties in general. This has been Armstrong’s
main focus since the late 1970s (e.g., Universals
Austin, J(ohn) L(angshaw)
Australasian philosophy
71
and Scientiﬁc Realism, 1978). There has been asso-
ciated discussion of the idea of a truthmaker – an
idea highlighted by C. B. Martin (e.g., “How It Is:
Entities, Absences, and Voids,” 1996), along with
John Fox (“Truthmaker,” 1987), John Bigelow
(The Reality of Numbers, 1988), and Armstrong
(Truth and Truthmakers, 2004). There has also
been prominent discussion, more generally, of
truth-at-all – realism or anti-realism about the
world and our semantic relationship to it; see,
e.g., Michael Devitt (Realism and Truth, 1984/
1991), Huw Price (Facts and the Function of Truth,
1988), Brian Ellis (Truth and Objectivity, 1990),
Bigelow
and
Robert
Pargetter
(Science
and
Necessity, 1990), and Barry Taylor (Models, Truth,
and Realism, 2006).
Such work has arisen with encouragement
from the distinctive tradition established by
Australasian logicians. From New Zealand, A. N.
Prior helped to initiate modern tense logic (e.g.,
Time and Modality, 1957). C. L. Hamblin (Fallacies,
1970)
heightened
contemporary
interest
in
informal logic. New Zealanders M. J. Cresswell
and G. E. Hughes wrote what was for many years
the best-known textbook on modal logic (An
Introduction to Modal Logic, 1972). Cresswell
enriched our formal understanding of language
(e.g., Logics and Languages, 1973), as did Richard
Routley and Leonard Goddard (The Logic of
Signiﬁcance and Context, 1973). Several philoso-
phers in the 1970s and onward – particularly
Richard and Valerie Routley, Robert Meyer,
Chris Mortensen (Inconsistent Mathematics, 1995),
and Ross Brady (Universal Logic, 2006) – enlarged
our conception of what relevance (or relevant)
logics could encompass. Graham Priest has
argued for dialetheism – there being true con-
tradictions (In Contradiction, 1987). Other signif-
icant contributors are Greg Restall and Lloyd
Humberstone.
Those various thoughts about mind, reality,
and logic have complemented well the strength
within Australasian philosophy of science: Brian
Ellis (e.g., Rational Belief Systems, 1979), Peter
Forrest (Quantum Metaphysics, 1988), Howard
Sankey (e.g., The Incommensurability Thesis, 1994),
Huw Price (Time’s Arrow and Archimedes’ Point,
1996), Paul Grifﬁths (e.g., What Emotions Really
Are, 1997), Mark Colyvan (The Indispensability of
Mathematics, 2001), Kim Sterelny (e.g., Thought in
a Hostile World, 2003), and Peter Godfrey-Smith
(Darwinian Populations and Natural Selection, 2009),
among others. There has been related engage-
ment with venerable questions about perception,
memory, testimony, knowledge, and justiﬁcation.
There was much debate in the 1960s about
perception,
between
Ellis,
Armstrong
(e.g.,
Perception and the Physical World, 1961), Max
Deutscher,
and
J.
L.
Mackie.
Later
came
Jackson’s representationalism (Perception, 1977).
On memory, Martin and Deutscher’s causal
account was inﬂuential (“Remembering,” 1966),
as was C. A. J. Coady’s non-reductionism about
testimony (Testimony, 1992). Armstrong devel-
oped one of the ﬁrst reliabilist theories of knowl-
edge
(Belief,
Truth
and
Knowledge,
1973).
Fallibilism has been defended in different ways,
such as by D. C. Stove (The Rationality of Induction,
1986) and the New Zealander Alan Musgrave
(Common Sense, Science and Scepticism, 1993). Alan
Hájek has advanced discussion of probability.
Australasian philosophy is not limited to meta-
physics, logic, philosophy of mind, philosophy of
science, and epistemology. Philosophy of religion is
well represented, for instance by Martin (Religious
Belief, 1959), John Passmore (The Perfectibility of
Man, 1970), H. J. McCloskey (God and Evil, 1974),
Robert Young (Freedom, Responsibility, and God,
1975), Mackie (The Miracle of Theism, 1982),
Graham Oppy (e.g., Ontological Arguments and
Belief in God, 1995), and Forrest (God Without the
Supernatural, 1996). Feminist philosophy has been
exempliﬁed by Genevieve Lloyd (The Man of
Reason, 1984/1993) and Moira Gatens (e.g.,
Feminism and Philosophy, 1991). There have
also been substantial contributions to ethics,
pure and applied. Smart defended utilitarianism
(Utilitarianism:
For
and
Against,
1973,
with
Bernard Williams). Peter Singer applied utilitari-
anism to non-human beings. His Animal Liberation
(1975) has had worldly inﬂuence far beyond aca-
demia. Helga Kuhse joined Singer in applying
more widely some of his utilitarian thinking
(e.g., Should the Baby Live? 1985). More recently,
the New Zealander Tim Mulgan (e.g., The Demands
of Consequentialism, 2001) has extended the theo-
retical bases of such discussions. Applied ethics
has had many Australian practitioners, such as
Coady, John Kleinig, McCloskey, and Garrett
Cullity (The Moral Demands of Afﬂuence, 2004).
Contemporary environmental philosophy, indeed,
was seeded partly by Richard Routley (later,
Richard Sylvan), Valerie Routley (later, Valerie
Plumwood), and Passmore (Man’s Responsibility
for Nature, 1974).
The New Zealanders Rosalind Hursthouse
(On Virtue Ethics, 1999) and Christine Swanton
(Virtue Ethics, 2003) have expanded our historical
and conceptual senses of what form a philosoph-
ical ethics can take. Australian contributors to
moral and political philosophy have included
McCloskey, Young (Personal Autonomy, 1986),
Australasian philosophy
Australasian philosophy
72
S. I. Benn (A Theory of Freedom, 1988), Michael
Smith (The Moral Problem, 1994), Philip Pettit
(e.g., Republicanism, 1997), and Jackson (From
Metaphysics to Ethics, 1998). Skeptical questions
about the reality of moral properties and the
possibility of moral knowledge were posed pro-
vocatively in Mackie’s Ethics (1977).
Running throughout some of these discussions
has been a methodology that is often called
the Canberra Plan. It is associated with ANU
(Australian National University) and some inﬂu-
ential philosophers, such as Jackson, Pettit, and
Smith. Its inspiration was David Lewis’s 1970s
work on theoretical terms, which applied partic-
ularly the idea of a Ramsey sentence. Canberra
planners seek to identify our most important
platitudes about a given phenomenon; then to
Ramsify those sentences, gaining in effect a the-
oretical description of the role that people in gen-
eral believe is played by the phenomenon. The
resulting conclusion is that the phenomenon
is whatever best plays that role. For example,
knowledge might be deemed to be whatever
best ﬁts the Ramsiﬁed role emerging from the
seemingly platitudinous intuitions sparked so
widely by Gettier cases.
Australasian philosophers have also contrib-
uted to the history of philosophy, especially
of empiricism. Armstrong wrote on Berkeley
and Locke; Martin joined him (e.g., “Substance
Substantiated,” 1980), as did Mackie (Problems
from Locke, 1976). On Hume, there have been
Passmore
(Hume’s
Intentions,
1952),
Stove
(Probability and Hume’s Inductive Scepticism, 1973),
Annette Baier (A Progress of Sentiments, 1991), and
Stephen
Buckle
(Hume’s
Enlightenment
Tract,
2001).
Stephen
Gaukroger
has
written
on
Descartes
(e.g.,
Cartesian
Logic,
1989),
Rae
Langton on Kant (Kantian Humility, 1998), Paul
Redding on Hegel (Hegel’s Hermeneutics, 1996),
Pettit on Hobbes (Made With Words, 2009), Peter
Anstey on Boyle (The Philosophy of Robert Boyle,
2000) and on Locke (e.g., John Locke and Natural
Philosophy,
2011),
and
Stewart
Candlish
on
Bradley and Russell (The Russell/Bradley Dispute
and Its Signiﬁcance for Twentieth-Century Philosophy,
2007).
John Anderson’s teaching at the University of
Sydney (1927–58) sparked the work of several
of the leading ﬁgures mentioned above. At the
University
of
Melbourne,
Douglas
Gasking
(during 1946–76) and A. C. Jackson (during
1948–66) were similarly inﬂuential. Enriching
Australasian
philosophy
has
been
the
Australasian Journal of Philosophy, founded in
1923 and still prominent.

Australian materialism.
See
AUSTRALASIAN
PHILOSOPHY, SMART.
Australian philosophy. See AUSTRALASIAN PHI-
LOSOPHY.
Austrian philosophy, a philosophical term of
art which, broadly construed, designates a philo-
sophical tradition that includes philosophers
who are either from Austria or inﬂuenced by
Austrian culture. (An overview is provided by
B. Smith, Austrian Philosophy: The Legacy of Franz
Brentano, 1994.) So understood, it comprises phi-
losophers ranging from Bolzano, Carnap, and
Musil to Popper and Wittgenstein. Whether
there is a distinctive Austrian tradition of philos-
ophy is controversial. Less controversial is the
view that there is a philosophical tradition that
originated in Vienna and centered on Brentano,
who taught in Vienna between 1874 and 1895.
He taught Husserl, Meinong, Twardowski, Chr.
von Ehrenfels, Carl Stumpf, and Anton Marty.
These philosophers either defend and develop
or
reject
and
modify
parts
of
Brentano’s
philosophy.
Brentano relied on four guiding assumptions:
(1) The proper method of philosophy is the
method of natural science. Like any natural sci-
ence, philosophy attempts to systematize data.
The difference is that, in general, philosophical
data are not gathered in experiments. Brentano
counts attentive introspection as an empirical
method that yields data for the (descriptive) psy-
chologist. (2) Psychology is the ﬁrst science
(Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, 1874,
Book I, 1 § 3). It is more valuable for human
progress than any other science. (3) Genetic and
descriptive psychology must be distinguished.
Descriptive psychology is related to genetic psy-
chology as anatomy is to physiology. Descriptive
psychology
(anatomy)
decomposes
the
mind
(body) into its basic elements (basic organs);
genetic psychology (physiology) develops a theory
of the functions of these elements (organs).
(4) Descriptive psychology is concerned with
the description and analysis of wholes. For exam-
ple, a mental life is a unity which the descriptive
psychologist decomposes into parts. These parts,
mental phenomena, are, again, unities with
parts. Brentano develops a theory of parts of
wholes to describe the mind. Husserl, Stumpf,
and others enrich and reﬁne this theory. While
Brentano’s students differ in their views on
core philosophical issues, they are uniﬁed in sub-
scribing to Brentano’s (1) to (4).
Australian materialism
Austrian philosophy
73
What are the core topics of the Brentano
school? Brentano’s main work, Psychology from
an Empirical Standpoint, proposed that intention-
ality is the most distinctive mark of the mental:
every mental phenomenon has an intentional
(in-existing) object: a presentation is a presenta-
tion of something, a judgment an afﬁrmation
of something, and so on. A further mark of the
mental is consciousness; i.e., one knows immedi-
ately that one thinks, feels, etc., if one does so.
Mental phenomena come in pairs; the most fun-
damental are love–hate and acknowledgment
(positive judgment)–rejection (negative judg-
ment).
The ﬁrst opposition is the basis of
Brentano’s theory of value. Something is valuable
(good) if it is correct to love it (see The Foundation
and Construction of Ethics, 1889). These basic
dichotomies are bones of contention in Austrian
philosophy. For example, Reinach (“On the
Theory of Negative Judgment,” 1911) aimed to
refute the view that judgment has a polar oppo-
site, ‘negative judgment’.
How do we know all this? We are immediately
aware of our present mental activity. But while
inner consciousness yields knowledge of mental
acts, we cannot observe these mental acts when we
have them (Brentano 1874, II, 2 § 9). Descriptive
psychologists must therefore rely on memory and
attention to acquire detailed knowledge of the
mental.
Brentano’s general epistemology is a variety
of
foundationalism:
knowledge
derived
from
evident judgments in evident steps. For Brentano,
evidence
guarantees
truth.
In
“Toward
an
Epistemological Assessment of Memory” (1866)
Meinong argued that memory beliefs have a differ-
ent form of evidence that is not truth-guaranteeing:
the evidence of surmise (Vermutungsevidenz).
Brentano made intentionality a core topic
in philosophy. An important contribution to
the
understanding
of
intentionality
in
the
Brentano school is Twardowski’s On the Content
and Object of Presentations (1894). Twardowski
appealed
to
Bolzano,
who
argued
in
his
Wissenschaftslehre (1837, 2d ed. Leipzig 1929)
that there are ideas with no object (the idea of
a golden mountain). For Brentanians this is
false: an idea is just something that presents
something. Twardowski argues (pro Brentano)
that everything that is the topic of a mental act is
an object, but (pro Bolzano) that not every
object is real. Bolzano’s logical realism that
acknowledges propositions and other logical
objects has had an important inﬂuence on sev-
eral philosophers in the Brentano school, most
importantly Husserl. Meinong further developed
the thesis that every intentional act has an object
by arguing that there are non-existent objects
(see his “On the Theory of Objects,” 1904).
Russell’s theory of deﬁnite descriptions is in part
motivated by his criticism of Meinong’s view in
“On Denoting” (1905).
The ﬁfth of Husserl’s Logical Investigations
(1900/1901, 2d ed. 1913) is a book-length dis-
cussion of Brentano’s view of intentionality. In it
Husserl changed tack and distinguished between
the matter, quality, and object of a mental act.
A mental phenomenon is intentional if, and only
if, it has a matter. The matter of an act can be
compared to a mode of presentation of an object.
The matter-object distinction allows Husserl to
say that mental phenomena such as imagining a
golden mountain are intentional, although there
is no such object as a golden mountain. Husserl’s
view is the starting point of what is now known as
phenomenology.
The primacy of psychology informs the work
of Brentanists in other areas of philosophy. For
example, Marty (in Untersuchungen zur Grundlegung
der allgemeinen Grammatik und Sprachphilosophie,
1908) developed a view of language on which
its function is to express one’s mental acts in
order to change the mental life of others.
Reinach investigated social acts like command-
ing, promising, etc. (“The A Priori Foundations of
Civil Law,” 1913). What is distinctive about these
acts is their directedness on other thinkers and
their mental acts.
The Brentano school forms a coherent and philo-
sophically inﬂuential tradition. Husserl founded
the phenomenological movement; Stumpf (see
the two volumes of his Tonpsychologie, 1883 and
1890) made important contributions to the psy-
chology of sound; Meinong and von Ehrenfels
made the birth of Gestalt psychology possible;
Twardowski was a major inﬂuence on Polish phi-
losophy as the founder of the Lvov school of
philosophy.
Vienna was the origin not only of the Brentano
school, but also of the Vienna Circle. The Vienna
Circle
–
well-known
members
are
Rudolf
Carnap, Hans Hahn, and Otto Neurath – revolved
around Moritz Schlick in the 1920s and 1930s. In
his General Theory of Knowledge (1918) Schlick
criticized the epistemology of the Brentano
school. This criticism is an integral part of the
Vienna Circle’s logical empiricism.
Ludwig Wittgenstein was in contact with the
Vienna Circle and inﬂuenced its philosophical
development (see Wittgenstein and the Vienna
Circle, Conversations Recorded by F. Waismann,
1978). However, neither Wittgenstein’s early
Austrian philosophy
Austrian philosophy
74
nor his late philosophy seems to have distinctive
Austrian roots.
See also BOLZANO, BRENTANO, CARNAP, GER-
MAN
PHILOSOPHY,
HUSSERL,
LOGICAL
POSITI-
VISM, MEINONG, POLISH PHILOSOPHY, SCHLICK,
VIENNA CIRCLE, WITTGENSTEIN.
M.Te.
autarkia, ancient Greek term meaning ‘self-
sufﬁciency’. Autarkia was widely regarded as a
mark of the human good, happiness (eudaimo-
nia). A life is self-sufﬁcient when it is worthy of
choice and lacks nothing. What makes a life self-
sufﬁcient – and thereby happy – was a matter of
controversy. Stoics maintained that the mere
possession of virtue would sufﬁce; Aristotle and
the Peripatetics insisted that virtue must be exer-
cised and even, perhaps, accompanied by mate-
rial goods. There was also a debate among later
Greek thinkers over whether a self-sufﬁcient life
is solitary or whether only life in a community
can be self-sufﬁcient. See also ARISTOTLE, STOI-
CISM.
E.C.H.
authenticity. See EXISTENTIALISM, HEIDEGGER.
authority, the right or power to impose and
enforce duties on others. Philosophical theories
of authority are normally concerned with this
kind of practical or normative authority. By con-
trast, epistemic or theoretical authority is the power
over opinion possessed by those with superior
knowledge or expertise in an area. In both cases,
a pronouncement by an accepted authority pro-
vides us with reasons that are peremptory and
content-independent. When a practical authority
tells us how to act or an epistemic authority tells us
what to believe, its status as an accepted authority
gives us reason to simply comply, even when we
cannot ourselves appreciate the reasons for its
actions.
De facto practical authorities are those having
the power (and claiming to have the right) to
impose duties and enforce obedience on others.
Many such authorities are also believed by (some
or all of) those subject to this power to exercise it
legitimately: to have the right to exercise it. In
these cases, the practical authority has a kind of
psychological authority over its subjects. Finally,
some authorities – that may or may not also
possess de facto authority – may in fact actually
have the right to impose and enforce duties, giv-
ing them de jure practical authority over others.
Modern philosophical theories of practical
authority developed against the background of
the Pauline doctrine (from Romans 13) that all
authority is instituted by God. That doctrine
motivated a conception of speciﬁcally political
authority – the divine right of kings – about
which many moderns were deeply skeptical. As
a result, attempts were made to distinguish the
basis of God’s authority from those of (what were
taken to be) the other paradigms of authority:
the authority of parents over their children, of
conquerors over the conquered, and of kings
(or governments) over their subjects. Modern
theories of political authority were then defended
that grounded it, e.g., in the consent of the gov-
erned (as in Locke) or in its necessity for doing
justice (as in Kant).
Contemporary theories of practical authority
have continued to focus primarily on the nature
and justiﬁcation of legal and political authority,
defending additional grounds for such authority
in, e.g., considerations of fairness or associative
responsibilities. But the perceived failure of these
(and other) accounts has also given rise to a sig-
niﬁcant skeptical tradition that either denies the
very possibility of de jure political authority or
denies that most (or any) de facto political author-
ities possess their authority legitimately.

avatar
(from
Sanskrit
avata¯ra),
in
Hindu
thought, any of the repeated “descents” of the
autarkia
avatar
75
Supreme Being into the physical world as an
animal, human being, or combination thereof,
to destroy evil and restore order. Predominantly
identiﬁed as the actions of the god Vishnu, these
entrances into the world indicate that Vishnu as
lord will adjust the cycle of karma. Its earliest
reference is in the Bhagavad Gita (150 B.C.),
where Krishna says that whenever dharma lan-
guishes he incarnates in age after age to destroy
evildoers and promote the good. Later lists of
avatars of Vishnu cite ten, twenty, or more,
with Krishna and the Buddha as famous exam-
ples. The inclusion of prominent local deities in
the list brought them under the inﬂuence of
Vishnu devotees, and today even Jesus and
Muhammad may be included. Modern philoso-
phers such as Radhakrishnan (1888–1975) rede-
ﬁne the concept non-theistically, identifying
an avatar as a human being who has attained
enlightenment.
