R.B.T.
free logic, a system of quantiﬁcation theory,
with or without identity, that allows for non-
denoting singular terms. In classical quantiﬁca-
tion theory, all singular terms (free variables and
individual constants) are assigned a denotation in
all models. But this condition appears counter-
intuitive when such systems are applied to natu-
ral language, where many singular terms seem to
be non-denoting (‘Pegasus’, ‘Sherlock Holmes’,
etc.). Various solutions of this problem have
been proposed, ranging from Frege’s chosen object
theory (assign an arbitrary denotation to each
non-denoting singular term) to Russell’s descrip-
tion theory (deny singular term status to most
expressions used as such in natural language,
and eliminate them from the “logical form” of
that language) to a weakening of the quantiﬁers’
“existential import,” which allows for denota-
tions to be possible, but not necessarily actual,
objects. All these solutions preserve the structure
of classical quantiﬁcation theory and make
adjustments at the level of application.
Free logic is a more radical solution: it allows
for legitimate singular terms to be denotation-
less, maintains the quantiﬁers’ existential import,
but modiﬁes both the proof theory and the
semantics
of ﬁrst-order
logic. Within proof
theory, the main modiﬁcation consists of elimi-
nating the rule of existential generalization,
which allows one to infer ‘There exists a ﬂying
horse’ from ‘Pegasus is a ﬂying horse’. Within
semantics, the main problem is giving truth con-
ditions for sentences containing non-denoting
singular terms, and there are various ways of
accomplishing this. Conventional semantics assigns
truth-values to atomic sentences containing non-
denoting singular terms by convention, and then
determines the truth-values of complex sen-
tences as usual. Outer domain semantics divides
the domain of interpretation into an inner and an
outer part, using the inner part as the range
of quantiﬁers and the outer part to provide for
“denotations” for non-denoting singular terms
(which are then not literally denotation-less, but
rather
left
without
an
existing
denotation).
Supervaluational semantics, when considering
a sentence A, assigns all possible combinations
of truth-values to the atomic components of
A
containing
non-denoting
singular
terms,
evaluates A on the basis of each of those combi-
nations, and then assigns to A the logical product
of all such evaluations. (Thus both ‘Pegasus ﬂies’
and ‘Pegasus does not ﬂy’ turn out to be truth-
valueless, but ‘Pegasus ﬂies or Pegasus does
not ﬂy’ turns out to be true since, whatever
truth-value is assigned to its atomic component
‘Pegasus ﬂies’, the truth-value for the whole sen-
tence is true.) A free logic is inclusive if it allows for
the possibility that the range of quantiﬁers
be empty (that there exists nothing at all); it is
exclusive otherwise.
See also FORMAL SEMANTICS, PROOF THEORY,
QUANTIFICATION.
E.Ben.
free rider, a person who beneﬁts from a social
arrangement without bearing an appropriate
share
of
the
burdens
of
maintaining
that
arrangement, e.g. one who beneﬁts from gov-
ernment services without paying taxes that
support them. The arrangements from which a
free rider beneﬁts may be either formal or infor-
mal. A cooperative arrangement that permits
free riders is likely to be unstable; parties to
the arrangement are unlikely to continue to
bear the burdens of maintaining it if others are
able to beneﬁt without doing their part. As a
result, it is common for cooperative arrange-
ments to include mechanisms to discourage
free riders, e.g. legal punishment, or in cases of
informal conventions the mere disapproval of
one’s peers. It is a matter of some controversy
as to whether it is always morally wrong to ben-
eﬁt from an arrangement without contributing
to its maintenance. See also JUSTICE, SOCIAL
CHOICE THEORY, UTILITARIANISM.
W.T.
free variable. See VARIABLE.
free will defense. See PHILOSOPHY OF RELIGION.
free will problem, the problem of the nature of
free agency and its relation to the origins and
conditions of responsible behavior. For those
who contrast ‘free’ with ‘determined’, a central
question is whether humans are free in what
they do or determined by external events beyond
their control. A related concern is whether respon-
sibility for an action requires that the agent, the
act, or the relevant decision be free. These, in turn,
direct attention to action, motivation, deliberation,
choice, and intention, and to the sense, if any, in
which our actions are under our control. Use of
‘free will’ is a matter of traditional nomenclature;
it is debated whether freedom is properly ascribed
381
free logic
free will problem
to the will or the agent, or to actions, choices,
deliberations, etc.
Controversy over conditions of responsible
behavior forms the predominant historical and
conceptual background of the free will problem.
Most who ascribe moral responsibility acknowl-
edge some sense in which agents must be free
in acting as they do; we are not responsible for
what we were forced to do or unable to avoid no
matter how hard we tried. But there are differing
accounts of moral responsibility and disagree-
ments about the nature and extent of practical
freedom. Accordingly, the free will problem cen-
ters on these questions: Does moral responsibility
require practical freedom? If so, what sort? Is
practical freedom consistent with the antecedent
determination of actions, thoughts, and charac-
ter? There is vivid debate about this last question.
Consider a woman deliberating about whom
to vote for. From her ﬁrst-person perspective,
she feels free to vote for any candidate and is
convinced that the selection is up to her. But,
viewing her eventual behavior as a segment of
larger natural and historical processes, many
would argue that underlying causes determine
her choice. Deciding whether the voter is free
depends on the precise meanings associated
with words and phrases like ‘free’, ‘determine’,
and ‘up to her’.
One thing (event, situation) determines another
if the latter is a consequence of it; e.g., the voter’s
hand movements are determined by her inten-
tion; and, as usually understood, determinism is
the thesis that whatever happens is causally
necessitated by antecedent events and circum-
stances. So construed, determinism apparently
implies that at any time the future is ﬁxed, with
no possibility of alternative development. Logical
versions of determinism declare each future
event to be determined by what is already true,
speciﬁcally by the truth that it will occur then.
Certain theological variants accept the predestina-
tion of all circumstances and events by a divine
being who knows in advance that they will
obtain.
Two elements are common to most interpreta-
tions of ‘free’. First, freedom requires an absence
of certain kinds of determination, and second,
one acts and chooses freely only if these endeav-
ors are, properly speaking, one’s own. From here,
accounts diverge. Some consider freedom (liberty)
of indifference or the contingency of alternative
actions critical, so that for the deliberating voter,
each choice is an open alternative: possible but
not yet necessitated. Indifference is also con-
strued as motivational equilibrium, a condition
some ﬁnd essential to the idea that a free choice
must be rational. Others focus on freedom (liberty)
of spontaneity, where the voter is free if she would
vote as she chooses or desires, a reading that
reﬂects the popular equation of freedom with
“doing what you want.” Associated with both
analyses is a third by which we act freely if we
exercise our control, implying not only respon-
siveness to intent, but abilities both to act and to
refrain from acting. A fourth view identiﬁes free-
dom with autonomy, the voter being autonomous:
self-determined, e.g., by her character, deeper
self, higher values, or informed reason. These
conceptions are compatible, and many accounts
of practical freedom include elements of each.
Determinism poses problems if practical free-
dom requires contingency (alternative possible
actions). Incompatibilism maintains that determin-
ism precludes freedom, though incompatibilists
differ as to whether everything is determined.
Those who accept determinism thereby endorse
hard determinism (associated with eighteenth-
century
thinkers
like
d’Holbach
and,
more
recently, certain behaviorists), on which freedom
is an illusion since behavior is brought about by
environmental and genetic factors. Some hard
determinists also deny the existence of moral
responsibility. At the opposite extreme, (meta-
physical) libertarianism asserts that people are
free and responsible and, a fortiori, that the past
does not determine a unique future, a position
some ﬁnd enhanced by developments in quan-
tum physics. Among adherents of this sort of
incompatibilism are those who advocate a free-
dom of indifference by describing responsible
choices as those that are undetermined by ante-
cedent circumstances (Epicureans). To rebut the
charge that choices, so construed, are random
and not really one’s “own,” some suggest that
several elements, including an agent’s reasons,
delimit the range of possibilities and inﬂuence
choices without necessitating them (Leibniz,
Robert Kane). Libertarians who espouse agency
causation, on the other hand, blend contingency
with autonomy in characterizing a free choice
as one that is determined by the agent, who
in turn is not caused to make it (Carneades,
Thomas Reid).
Unwilling to abandon practical freedom or to
view a lack of determination as either necessary
or desirable for responsibility, many philosophers
take practical freedom and responsibility to be
consistent with determinism, thereby endorsing
compatibilism. Those who also accept determinism
advocate what William James called soft determin-
ism. Its supporters include some who identify
382
free will problem
free will problem
freedom with autonomy (Stoics, Spinoza) and
others who champion freedom of spontaneity
(Hobbes, Locke, Hume). The latter speak of liberty
as the power of doing or refraining from an action
according to what one wills, so that by choosing
otherwise one would have done otherwise. An
agent fails to have liberty when constrained:
either prevented from acting as one chooses or
compelled to act in a manner contrary to what
one wills. Extending this model, liberty is also
diminished when one is caused to act in a way
one would not otherwise prefer, either to avoid
a greater danger (coercion) or because there is
deliberate interference with the envisioning of
alternatives (manipulation).
Compatibilists
have
shown
considerable
ingenuity in responding to criticisms that they
have ignored freedom of choice or the need for
open alternatives. Some apply the spontaneity,
control, or autonomy models to decisions, so that
the voter chooses freely if her decision accords
with her desires, is under her control, or con-
forms to her higher values, deeper character, or
informed reason. Others challenge the idea that
responsibility requires alternative possibilities of
action. In so-called Frankfurt-style cases agents act
in accord with their desires and choices, but
because of a counterfactual intervener – a mech-
anism that would have prevented doing any
alternative action had they shown signs of acting
differently – they could not have done otherwise.
Frankfurt’s intuition is that the agent is as respon-
sible as he would have been even had there been
no intervener and, thus, that responsible action
does not require alternative possibilities. Critics
have challenged the details of the Frankfurt-style
cases by either denying the intuition or by grant-
ing that its appeal rests on the recognition of prior
alternatives.
A different compatibilist strategy recognizes
the need for open alternatives and employs
versions of the indifference model in describing
practical freedom. Choices are free if they are
contingent relative to certain subsets of circum-
stances, e.g. those the agent is or claims to be
cognizant of, with the openness of alternatives
grounded in what one can do or choose “for all
one knows.”
Opponents of compatibilism charge that these
reﬁnements leave agents subject to external
determination. Some advance the manipulation
argument: even a covertly manipulated agent
could satisfy compatibilist conditions on free
agency, contrary to what seems plausible. Some
compatibilists dispute the analogy; others argue
that manipulation does not, per se, rule out
responsibility. A more general objection to com-
patibilism is given by the consequence argument
(so called by van Inwagen): if everything were
determined by factors beyond one’s control, then
one’s acts, choices, and character would also be
beyond one’s control, and consequently agents
would never be free and hence never responsible.
Such
reasoning
usually
employs
principles
asserting the closure of the practical modalities
(ability, control, avoidability, inevitability, etc.)
under consequence relations. However, there is
reason to suppose that the sort of control required
by responsibility involves the agent’s sense of
what can be accomplished. Since cognitive states
are typically not closed under consequence, the
closure principles underlying the consequence
argument are disputable.
See also
CAUSATION,
DETERMINISM,
DIMIN-
ISHED CAPACITY, FRANKFURT CASES, MIND ARGU-
MENT.
T.K.
Frege, Gottlob (1848–1925), German mathe-
matician and philosopher, a founder of modern
mathematical logic, an advocate of logicism,
and a major source of twentieth-century analytic
philosophy.
He
directly
inﬂuenced
Russell,
Wittgenstein, and Carnap. Frege’s distinction
between the sense and the reference of linguistic
expressions continues to be debated.
His ﬁrst publication in logic was his strikingly
original 1879 Begriffsschrift (“Concept Notation”).
Here he devised a formal language whose central
innovation is the quantiﬁer-variable notation to
express generality; he set forth in this language a
version of second-order quantiﬁcational logic
that he used to develop a logical deﬁnition of
the ancestral of a relation. Frege invented his
Begriffsschrift in order to circumvent drawbacks
of the use of colloquial language to state proofs.
Colloquial language is irregular, unperspicuous,
and ambiguous in its expression of logical rela-
tionships. Moreover, logically crucial features of
the content of statements may remain tacit and
unspoken. It is thus impossible to determine
exhaustively the premises on which the conclu-
sion of any proof conducted within ordinary lan-
guage depends. Frege’s Begriffsschrift is to force
the explicit statement of the logically relevant
features of any assertion. Proofs in the system
are limited to what can be obtained from a
body of evidently true logical axioms by means
of a small number of truth-preserving notational
manipulations (inference rules). Here is the ﬁrst
hallmark of Frege’s view of logic: his formulation
of logic as a formal system and the ideal of explic-
itness and rigor that this presentation subserves.
383
Frege, Gottlob
Frege, Gottlob
Although the formal exactitude with which he
formulates logic makes possible the metamathe-
matical investigation of formalized theories, he
showed almost no interest in metamathematical
questions. He intended the Begriffsschrift to be used.
How, though, does Frege conceive the subject
matter of logic? His orientation in logic is shaped
by his anti-psychologism, his conviction that psy-
chology has nothing to do with logic. He took his
notation to be a full-ﬂedged language in its own
right. The logical axioms do not mention objects
or properties whose investigation pertains to
some special science; and Frege’s quantiﬁers are
unrestricted. Laws of logic are, as he says, the
laws of truth, and these are the most general
truths. He envisioned the supplementation of
the logical vocabulary of the Begriffsschrift with
the basic vocabulary of the special sciences. In
this way the Begriffsschrift affords a framework
for the completely rigorous deductive develop-
ment of any science whatsoever. This resolutely
non-psychological universalist view of logic as
the most general science is the second hallmark
of Frege’s view of logic. This universalist view
distinguishes his approach sharply from the
coeval algebra of logic approach of Boole and
Ernst
Schröder.
Wittgenstein,
both
in
the
Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) and in later
writings, is very critical of Frege’s universalist
view. Logical positivism – most notably Carnap
in The Logical Syntax of Language (1934) – rejected
it as well. Frege’s universalist view is also distinct
from more contemporary views. With his view of
quantiﬁers as intrinsically unrestricted, he saw
little point in talking of varying interpretations
of a language, believing that such talk is a con-
fused way of getting at what is properly said
by means of second-order generalizations. In
particular, the semantical conception of logical
consequences that becomes prominent in logic
after Gödel’s and Tarski’s work is foreign to Frege.
Frege’s work in logic was prompted by an
inquiry into the ultimate foundation of arith-
metic truths. He criticized J. S. Mill’s empiricist
attempt to ground knowledge of the arithmetic of
the positive integers inductively in our manipu-
lations of small collections of things. He also
rejected crudely formalist views that take pure
mathematics to be a sort of notational game. In
contrast to these views and Kant’s, he hoped to
use his Begriffsschrift to deﬁne explicitly the basic
notions of arithmetic in logical terms and to
deduce the basic principles of arithmetic from
logical axioms and these deﬁnitions. The explicit-
ness and rigor of his formulation of logic will
guarantee that there are no implicit extralogical
premises on which the arithmetical conclusions
depend. Such proofs, he believed, would show
arithmetic to be analytic, not synthetic as Kant
had claimed. However, Frege redeﬁned ‘analytic’
to mean ‘provable from logical laws’ (in his rather
un-Kantian sense of ‘logic’) and deﬁnitions.
Frege’s strategy for these proofs rests on an
analysis of the concept of cardinal number that
he presented in his non-technical 1884 book, The
Foundations of Arithmetic. Frege, attending to the
use of numerals in statements like ‘Mars has two
moons’, argued that it contains an assertion
about a concept, that it asserts that there are
exactly two things falling under the concept
‘Martian moon’. He also noted that both numer-
als in these statements and those of pure arith-
metic play the logical role of singular terms, his
proper names. He concluded that numbers are
objects, so that a deﬁnition of the concept of
number must then specify what objects numbers
are. He observed that
(1) the number of F = the number of G just in
case there is a one-to-one correspondence
between the objects that are F and those
that are G.
The right-hand side of (1) is statable in purely
logical terms. As Frege recognized, thanks to the
deﬁnition of the ancestral of a relation, (1) suf-
ﬁces in the second-order setting of the Begriffsschrift
for the derivation of elementary arithmetic. The
vindication of his logicism requires, however, the
logical deﬁnition of the expression ‘the number
of’. He sharply criticized the use in mathematics
of any notion of set or collection that views a set
as built up from its elements. However, he
assumed that, corresponding to each concept,
there is an object, the extension of the concept.
He took the notion of an extension to be a logical
one, although one to which the notion of a con-
cept is prior. He adopted as a fundamental logical
principle the ill-fated biconditional: the extension
of F = the extension of G just in case every F is G,
and vice versa. If this principle were valid, he
could exploit the equivalence relation over con-
cepts that ﬁgure in the right-hand side of (1) to
identify the number of F with a certain extension
and thus obtain (1) as a theorem. In The Basic Laws
of Arithmetic (Vol. 1, 1893; Vol. 2, 1903) he
formalized putative proofs of basic arithmetical
laws
within
a
modiﬁed
version
of
the
Begriffsschrift that included a generalization of
the law of extensions. However, Frege’s law of
extensions, in the context of his logic, is incon-
sistent, leading to Russell’s paradox, as Russell
communicated to Frege in 1902. Frege’s attempt
384
Frege, Gottlob
Frege, Gottlob
to establish logicism was thus, on its own terms,
unsuccessful.
In Begriffsschrift Frege rejected the thesis
that every un-compound sentence is logically
segmented into a subject and a predicate. Later,
he said that his approach in logic was distinctive
in starting not from the synthesis of concepts
into judgments, but with the notion of truth
and that to which this notion is applicable,
the judgeable contents or thoughts that are
expressed by statements. Although he said that
truth is the goal of logic, he did not think that we
have a grasp of the notion of truth that is inde-
pendent of logic. He eschewed a correspondence
theory of truth, embracing instead a redundancy
view of the truth-predicate. For Frege, to call
truth the goal of logic points toward logic’s con-
cern with inference, with the recognition-of-
the-truth (judging) of one thought on the basis
of
the
recognition-of-the-truth
of
another.
This recognition-of-the-truth-of is not verbally
expressed by a predicate, but rather in the asser-
tive force with which a sentence is uttered.
The starting point for logic is then reﬂection on
elementary
inference
patterns
that
analyze
thoughts and reveal a logical segmentation in
language.
This starting point, and the fusion of logical and
ontological categories it engenders, is arguably
what Frege is pointing toward by his enigmatic
context principle in Foundations: only in the context
of a sentence does a word have a meaning. He
views sentences as having a function-argument
segmentation like that manifest in the terms of
arithmetic, e.g. (3 × 4) + 2. Truth-functional
inference patterns, like modus ponens, isolate sen-
tences as logical units in compound sentences.
Leibniz’s law – the substitution of one name
for another in a sentence on the basis of an
equation – isolates proper names. Proper names
designate
objects.
Predicates,
obtainable
by
removing proper names from sentences, desig-
nate concepts. The removal of a predicate from
a sentence leaves a higher-level predicate that
signiﬁes a second-level concept under which
ﬁrst-level concepts fall. An example is the uni-
versal quantiﬁer over objects: it designates a
second-level concept under which a ﬁrst-level
concept falls, if every object falls under it. Frege
takes each ﬁrst-level concept to be determinately
true or false of each object. Vague predicates,
like ‘is bald’, thus fail to signify concepts. This
requirement of concept determinacy is a product
of Frege’s construal of quantiﬁcation over objects
as intrinsically unrestricted. Thus, concept deter-
minacy is simply a form of the law of the excluded
middle: for any concept F and any object x, either
x is F or x is not F.
Frege elaborates and modiﬁes his basic logical
ideas in three seminal papers from 1891 to
1892, “Function and Concept,” “On Concept
and Object,” and “On Sense and Meaning.” In
“Function and Concept,” Frege sharpens his con-
ception of the function-argument structure of
language. He introduces the two truth-values,
the True and the False, and maintains that
sentences are proper names of these objects.
Concepts become functions that map objects to
either the True or the False. The course-of-values
of a function is introduced as a generalization of
the notion of an extension. Generally, then, an
object is anything that might be designated by a
proper name. There is nothing more basic to be
said by way of elucidating what an object is.
Similarly, ﬁrst-level functions are what are
designated by the expressions that result from
removing
names
from
compound
proper
names.
Frege
calls
functions
unsaturated
or
incomplete, in contrast to objects, which are satu-
rated. Proper names and function names are not
intersubstitutable, so that the distinction between
objects and functions is a type-theoretic, catego-
rial distinction. No function is an object; no func-
tion name designates an object; there are no
quantiﬁers that simultaneously generalize over
both functions and concepts.
Just here Frege’s exposition of his views, if not
the views themselves, encounters a difﬁculty. In
explaining his views, he uses proper names of the
form ‘the concept F’ to talk about concepts; and in
contrasting unsaturated functions with saturated
objects, appears to generalize over both with a
single quantiﬁer. Benno Kerry, a contemporary
of Frege, charged Frege’s views with inconsis-
tency. Since the phrase ‘the concept horse’ is a
proper name, it must designate an object. On
Frege’s view, it follows that the concept ‘horse’
is not a concept, but an object, an apparent incon-
sistency. Frege responded to Kerry’s criticism in
“On Concept and Object.” He embraced Kerry’s
paradox, denying that it represents a genuine
inconsistency, while admitting that his remarks
about the function-object distinction are, as the
result of an unavoidable awkwardness of lan-
guage, misleading. Frege maintained that the dis-
tinction between function and object is logically
simple and so cannot be properly deﬁned.
His remarks on the distinction are informal
hand waving designed to elucidate what is cap-
tured within the Begriffsschrift by the difference
between proper names and function names
together with their associated distinct quantiﬁers.
385
Frege, Gottlob
Frege, Gottlob
Frege’s handling of the function-object distinc-
tion is a likely source for Wittgenstein’s say-
show distinction in the Tractatus.
At the beginning of “On Sense and Meaning,”
Frege distinguishes between the reference or
meaning (Bedeutung) of a proper name and its
sense (Sinn). He observes that the sentence
‘The Morning Star is identical with the Morning
Star’ is a trivial instance of the principle of iden-
tity. In contrast, the sentence ‘The Morning Star
is identical with the Evening Star’ expresses a
substantive astronomical discovery. The two
sentences thus differ in what Frege called their
cognitive value: someone who understood both
might believe the ﬁrst and doubt the second.
This difference cannot be explained in terms of
any difference in reference between names in
these sentences. Frege explained it in terms of a
difference between the senses expressed by ‘the
Morning Star’ and ‘the Evening Star’. In posthu-
mously published writings, he indicated that the
sense-reference distinction extends to function
names as well. In this distinction, Frege extends
to names the notion of the judgeable content
expressed by a sentence: the sense of a name
is the contribution that the name makes to the
thought expressed by sentences in which it
occurs. Simultaneously, in classifying sentences
as proper names of truth-values, he applies to
sentences the notion of a name’s referring to
something. Frege’s function-argument view of
logical segmentation constrains his view of both
the meaning and the sense of compound names:
the substitution for any name occurring in a com-
pound expression of a name with the same refer-
ence (sense) yields a new compound expression
with the same reference (sense) as the original.
Frege advances several theses about sense
that individually and collectively have been a
source of debate in philosophy of language.
First, the sense of an expression is what is grasped
by anyone who understands it. Despite the con-
nection between understanding and sense, Frege
provides no account of synonymy, no identity
criteria for senses. Second, the sense of an expres-
sion is not something psychological. Senses are
objective. They exist independently of anyone’s
grasping them; their availability to different
thinkers is a presupposition for communication
in science. Third, the sense expressed by a name
is a mode of presentation of the name’s reference.
Here
Frege’s
views
contrast
with
Russell’s.
Corresponding to Frege’s thoughts are Russell’s
propositions. In The Principles of Mathematics
(1903), Russell maintained that the meaningful
words in a sentence designate things, properties,
and relations that are themselves constituents of
the proposition expressed by the sentence. For
Frege, our access through judgment to objects
and functions is via the senses that are expressed
by names that mean these items. These senses,
not the items they present, occur in thoughts.
Names expressing different senses may refer to
the same item; and some names, while express-
ing a sense, refer to nothing. Any compound
name containing a name that has a sense, but
lacks a reference, itself lacks a meaning. A person
may fully understand an expression without
knowing whether it means anything and without
knowing whether it designates what another
understood name does. Fourth, the sense ordina-
rily expressed by a name is the reference of
the name, when the name occurs in indirect dis-
course. Although the Morning Star is identical
with the Evening Star, the inference from the
sentence ‘Smith believes that the Morning Star
is a planet’ to ‘Smith believes that the Evening
Star is a planet’ is not sound. Frege, however,
accepts Leibniz’s law without restriction. He
accordingly
takes
such
seeming
failures
of
Leibniz’s law to expose a pervasive ambiguity in
colloquial language: names in indirect discourse
do not designate what they designate outside of
indirect discourse. The fourth thesis is offered as
an explanation of this ambiguity.
See also LOGICISM, MEANING, RUSSELL, SET-
THEORETIC PARADOXES, SET THEORY.
T.R.
Frege-Geach point. See GEACH.
Frege-Geach problem, also known as the
embedding problem, focuses on puzzles for non-
cognitivist moral semantics, arising from the
ordinary linguistic behavior of moral terms and
sentences. Moral sentences seem to have the
same meaning even when embedded in logical
contexts where they are not asserted, and they
seem to function just like ordinary declarative
sentences in logical inferences. For example, ‘It
is wrong to lie’ seems to have the same meaning
whether asserted alone or ﬁguring as part of the
conditional ‘If it is wrong to lie, then it is wrong
to get your little brother to lie’. Yet it is hard to
see how it could have the same meaning on a
noncognitivist account where ‘It is wrong to lie’
simply
expresses
disapproval
of
lying:
one
needn’t express any such disapproval of lying in
asserting the conditional. Similarly, we appa-
rently may infer logically from the above two
claims that it is wrong to get your little brother
to lie. Yet this is puzzling on a noncognitivist
account where ‘It is wrong to lie’ does not express
386
Frege-Geach point
Frege-Geach problem
a proposition and again seems to change meaning
between the non-embedded and embedded uses.
See also EMOTIVISM, ETHICS, GEACH.
W.F.
French personalism, a Christian socialism
stressing social activism and personal responsibil-
ity, the theoretical basis for the Christian work-
ers’ Esprit movement begun in the 1930s by
Emmanuel
Mounier
(1905–50),
a
Christian
philosopher and activist. Inﬂuenced by both
the religious existentialism of Kierkegaard and
the radical social action called for by Marx
and in part taking direction from the earlier
work of Charles Péguy, the movement strongly
opposed fascism and called for worker solidarity
during the 1930s and 1940s. It also urged a
more humane treatment of France’s colonies.
Personalism allowed for a Christian socialism
independent of both more conservative Christian
groups and the Communist labor unions and
party. Its most important book is Mounier’s
Personalism. The quarterly journal Esprit has
regularly
published
contributions
of
leading
French and international thinkers. Such well-
known Christian philosophers as Henry Duméry,
Marcel, Maritain, and Ricoeur were attracted to
the movement. See also FRENCH PHILOSOPHY,
MARCEL, MARITAIN, PERSONALISM, RICOEUR.
J.Bi.
French philosophy, the philosophy produced
by thinkers working in the French language,
beginning with the essay as a new literary genre
created by Michel de Montaigne (1533–92),
and with the championing by René Descartes
(1596–1650) of a new method of inquiry to sup-
plant the approaches of Scholasticism. The work
of Maine de Biran (1766–1824) provides a prism
through which we can look both forward and
backward; it provides useful perspectives on the
French philosophical tradition as a whole. He
spoke of “a thread which guides our inquiry” –
our awareness of willed effort and its central role
in philosophy. Though Biran’s name is some-
times associated with French “personalism,” his
work had a broader reach than that associated
with the personalists; in particular, he gave a
signiﬁcant role to animal physiology as illuminat-
ing the processes that underlie conscious life and
of which we may have a partial or subconscious
awareness, or indeed none at all. To these
“two lives” – the passive animal life and the
active conscious life – he later added a higher
life of passivity, the life of the spirit. This too was
to be investigated by what he called “experimen-
tal psychology,” meaning a method based on
analysis of our conscious life. Though his “life of
the spirit” pointed forward to French spiritualism,
Biran himself cannot be called a “spiritualist”
thinker.
Aristotle’s executive model of the will as that
which enables the passage from practical reason-
ing into action was widely inﬂuential in several
traditions, in Arabic philosophy initially and then
in various European traditions, including that
of France. For many, the will was just one
component of psychological, metaphysical, or
theological theory and not the cornerstone that
Biran later claimed it to be. This model could raise
conceptual problems, illustrated by the conun-
drum known as “Buridan’s ass,” named for the
fourteenth-century French scholastic Buridan: if
a hungry ass is equidistant from two indistin-
guishable piles of hay, will it die of hunger,
since it has no reason to go for one rather
than the other? Three centuries later, in his
Dictionnaire, Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) treated
Buridan’s ass as a sophism, which enabled
Buridan to win a debate. Whichever answer is
given, the respondent can be pushed into
paradox. Three centuries later, Sartre (1905–80)
told a related story, in “Existentialism Is a
Humanism,” about a young man in occupied
France: should he join the Free French or stay
home to attend his ailing mother? For Sartre, no
preexisting principles, commitments, or desires
could determine the choice: the act of choice itself
is sovereign. On this existentialist view, the ass
problem would not get off the ground.
Empiricism was also a concern of Biran’s. He
was, at least early in his philosophizing, an
avowed empiricist; but although he considered
Locke correct in identifying reﬂection as well as
sensation as a source of knowledge, he thought
Locke wrong in thinking that it gave us access to
purely inner facts. This just led to a new Cartesian
trap. What reﬂection actually gives us, Biran
claimed, is a primitive volitional fact – a particular
relation between ourselves and the world. It
is important to emphasize how radical a break
this made with Cartesian dualism. For despite
Descartes’s insistence that I am not in my body
as a pilot is in a ship and his emphasis on
the “substantial union” of body and soul/mind
(anima/esprit), these gestures remain nominal
when set against his resolute dualism. That dual-
ism made incomprehensible what Biran later
claimed to be the primitive fact of our experience,
the experience of willed action or effort.
Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), an admirer
of Descartes, went still further. Where Descartes
in various ways held onto mind/body interaction,
387
French personalism
French philosophy
Malebranche insisted that God alone was the true
cause of anything that happened. Though we like
to think that in the world A causes B, in truth A is
merely the occasion for B. God alone is the cause
of A and of B. In a late version of Malebranche’s
De la recherche de la vérité, he explicitly addressed
the feeling of effort which was to be Biran’s cen-
tral concern, claiming that it was a purely inner
awareness, without connection to any knowl-
edge of bodily mechanisms. This is precisely
what Biran was to deny.
For Biran, the revolution in the natural scien-
ces brought about by Newton was also of major
importance. However, it had led many to attempt
to apply supposedly similar methods directly
to living creatures, giving rise to various materi-
alistic explanatory exercises of which Julien
Offray
de
La
Mettrie’s (1709–51) L’Homme
Machine (1748) and Paul-Henri Dietrich, baron
d’Holbach’s
(1723–89)
Système
de
la
nature
(1770) are emblematic examples. Biran’s view
of such enterprises becomes clear in something
he
said
about
Pierre-Jean-Georges
Cabanis
(1757–1808): “No paradox can surprise us from
a man who goes so far as to assure us that
‘the brain should be considered as a particular
organ specially destined to produce thought’ . . .
concluding that the brain digests impressions, that
it effects organically the secretion of thought. . . .
Cabanis transforms a metaphor into a physical
thesis. . . . To say that the brain ﬁlters thoughts is
certainly the greatest absurdity.” For Biran, this
awareness of willed effort should be our starting
point in the human sciences. At all events, Biran’s
revision of traditional empiricism turned out
to be drastic: despite his own immersion in the
sciences of his day, it led later French philosoph-
ical thought in broadly anti-scientistic directions,
with a number of exceptions, such as Comte
and Bergson. In particular, his relational view of
the primitive relational fact of willed effort was a
precursor of phenomenology. Maurice Merleau-
Ponty (1908–61), in The Incarnate Subject, elabo-
rated this idea in his own way, referring to
Malebranche, Biran, and Bergson as ancestral.
The foundational privilege given by Biran to
relational facts also preﬁgures structuralism, in
which the identity of an item is given by its rela-
tion to other items rather than in itself, as many
earlier and later empiricists believed. This idea
was signiﬁcant for later French thought, and
indeed more widely. Structuralist movements
arose in mathematics (with a group of mainly
French mathematicians writing under the pseu-
donym “Nicolas Bourbaki”, numerous volumes
being published between 1935 and 1998), in
linguistics (Ferdinand de Saussure, 1857–1913,
and others), and in the social sciences and philos-
ophy (about which more to follow).
Biran himself, however, did not generalize in
this way from the relational structure that was his
own starting point in psychology. This starting
point, indeed, did not stand by itself, since the
experience of willed effort did not exist in a vac-
uum. For the effort can be a bodily effort, and
thus our bodily awareness is also invoked. Biran
considered that our conscious life, given to us
through “reﬂection,” had a subconscious under-
layer, which he sometimes called our uncon-
scious “animal life.” He wondered whether
someday a “new Columbus” would explore it.
These are noteworthy preﬁgurations of the
work of Freud and the whole movement of
psychoanalysis, which
became
important
in
later French thought.
These points are connected with a long-
standing question in the history of French
philosophy: what method should be used in
philosophical inquiry? The skeptical approach,
since antiquity, had been to protect us from
unjustiﬁable theoretical assumptions by mar-
shaling arguments against as well as for them.
We ﬁnd echoes of this in Montaigne, a “rustic
skeptic.” Montaigne, like Descartes, was well
read in the ancient Skeptics such as Pyrrho and
Sextus Empiricus. But where for Descartes
skepticism was a tool of inquiry, for Montaigne
it was a tool for living. Descartes used his
method of doubt to place philosophical and
mathematical
knowledge
on
an
absolutely
secure foundation. Going further, he sought
to unify all knowledge, and thus proposed a
universal method of inquiry that would guide
the right conduct of reason as it sought truth in
any of the sciences. The question of method is
ancient. Aristotle in particular was a method-
ologist with substantial inﬂuence in French
philosophy (Bergson’s secondary doctoral the-
sis, Quid Aristoteles de loco senserit, was about
Aristotle’s treatment of place). Aristotle held
that certain terms, such as those of logic, math-
ematics, and value, instead of being “equivo-
cal,” with meanings internal to each separate
discipline, were in fact univocal. This view has
long echoes in French thought.
As early as Pierre Abélard (1079–1142), we
ﬁnd not only methodical doubt, but also a con-
cern with logic and dialectic. And Descartes’s
concern with method was not unrelated to
his important mathematical work. In fact, math-
ematics burgeoned in the seventeenth century.
Blaise Pascal (1623–62) made important advances,
388
French philosophy
French philosophy
though he considered that zero and negative
numbers were not really numbers at all, while
the conjecture of Pierre de Fermat (1601–65),
known as his “last theorem,” was only recently
proved by Andrew Wiles (1953).
We should also mention here the term-logic of
Port-Royal (La logique, ou l’art de penser, 1662).
Antoine Arnauld (1612–94), of Port-Royal, was
another admirer of Descartes. Despite disagree-
ing with Descartes’s philosophical position on a
number of matters, particularly theological ones,
he attempted to take Descartes’s advocacy of a
general method of inquiry much further.
The eighteenth-century Enlightenment.
The eighteenth century brought a great break.
French thinkers previously operated within a
more or less unchallenged political and religious
framework
(despite
various
signiﬁcant
skir-
mishes). But the Enlightenment changed that.
The ﬁrst major ﬁgure was Montesquieu (1689–
1755), the ﬁrst signiﬁcant social-political and
legal historian and commentator. He stated that
“government should be set up so that no man
need be afraid of another.” He admired the liberty
of the British under their new system of social
and political checks and balances. Though he
did not support the American Revolution, he
remained greatly respected in America, in part
for his articulation of a theory of the separation
of powers between executive, legislative, and
judicial
bodies.
Montesquieu was
the most
frequently quoted authority on government and
politics
in
colonial
pre-revolutionary
British
America, and was cited more often by the
American founders than any source except the
Bible. His most important book, The Spirit of the
Laws (1748), although placed by the Catholic
Church on the Index of Prohibited Books,
remains a classic in the history of political theory
and jurisprudence.
Voltaire (1694–1778), among the greatest of
French writers, explicitly attacked Catholicism
and advocated freedom of religion and expres-
sion. He wrote widely on numerous subjects and
in different literary forms. He was known for
his defense of religious tolerance and advocacy
of respect for human rights, as well as for his
satirical polemics, particularly his attacks on
French institutions, as exempliﬁed in his master-
work Candide, or Optimism (1759), which includes
a ruthlessly sarcastic treatment of Leibniz’s idea
of preestablished harmony.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–78) is especially
known for his notion of the social contract and of
the noble savage in two major works of political
philosophy: A Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
(1755) and The Social Contract (1762). His novel
Émile: or, On Education (1762) explores basic
questions concerning the relation between the
individual and society in the context of address-
ing the question of how to educate the individual
for citizenship, while his Confessions, published
posthumously in two parts, 1782 and 1789, is
often cited as the ﬁrst modern autobiography. He
contributed numerous articles to the Encyclopédie.
He later contended that different religions were of
equal value, so long as they led to virtue. The
result was that he (and his books) were banned
in France and in Geneva.
Denis Diderot (1713–84) was imprisoned in
Vincennes for his Letter on the Blind, which pre-
sented a materialist view. He was visited in prison
by his friend Rousseau (not himself a materialist).
Diderot recanted and was released. He then
became free for the work for that, with Jean le
Rond d’Alembert (1717–83), he is particularly
known, the Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné
des sciences, des arts et des métiers. This was contro-
versial from the beginning, and was suppressed
by decree in 1859, two decades after its initiation,
though the work continued clandestinely. When
completed, it consisted of more than 70,000
articles by more than 140 contributors, appeared
in 28 volumes between 1751 and 1772, and
stands as one of the major accomplishments of
the French Enlightenment.
Nicolas de Condorcet (1743–94) was a philos-
opher, mathematician, and political and educa-
tional reformer whose best-known work, Sketch
for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human
Mind (1795), in arguing for the ultimate perfect-
ibility of the human race, stands as an exemplar
of the Enlightenment. He was equally well
known for his application of probability theory
to political elections in his formulation of a
voting paradox, known as the Condorcet paradox,
which demonstrated that majority preferences
become intransitive with three or more options –
it is possible for a certain electorate in a single
ballot to express a preference for A over B,
a preference for B over C, and a preference for
C over A. A champion of liberal economics and
politics, Cordorcet was a strong proponent of
free and equal public education, equal rights
for women, including the right to vote, and the
abolition of slavery. The ideas of these ﬁve
enlightenment ﬁgures, indeed, ﬁnd a proximate
culmination in the French Revolution.
Two other thinkers should be mentioned.
First, Étienne Bonnot de Condillac (1715–80) is
viewed as the person who introduced the ideas of
389
French philosophy
French philosophy
British empiricism, and of Locke in particular, to
France. This is not incorrect, but there are impor-
tant qualiﬁcations. The main one is that whereas
Locke regarded ideas as existing furniture of the
mind, and language simply as a device by which
these ideas could be transmitted to others,
Condillac’s sensationalism contended that signs
(or language) played a constitutive role in the
formation of ideas. Among his most important
works are the Essay on the Origin of Human
Knowledge (1746) and the Treatise on Sensations
(1754). Second, Destutt de Tracy (1754–1836)
took part in the French Revolution, but then
settled in Auteuil in the company of Cabanis
and Condorcet and, during the Reign of Terror,
was imprisoned for almost one year. During
this time, he turned from the natural sciences
to philosophy and began his study of the sensa-
tionalism of Condillac and Locke, ultimately
concluding that there are four principal kinds
of conscious behavior – perception, memory,
judgment, and will – each comprising various
combinations of sensations. Destutt de Tracy is
perhaps best known as the founder a rather
short-lived school of philosophical thought he
called “idéologie” – the science of ideas.
The nineteenth century: socialism, positi-
vism,
spiritualism.
Philosophy
in
France
pursued three main programs in the ﬁrst half
of the nineteenth century: the utopian socialism
of
Claude
Henri
Saint-Simon
(1760–1825),
François-Marie-Charles
Fourier
(1772–1837),
and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809–65); the
eclecticism
of
Victor
Cousin
(1792–1867),
Pierre-Paul
Royer-Collard
(1763–1845),
and
Théodore Jouffroy (1796–1842); and the positi-
vism of Auguste Comte (1798–1857). Among
these, Comte had the most lasting inﬂuence.
Comte is perhaps best known as the founder of
sociology, which itself grew out of his positive
philosophy. His positivism blends an empiricist
commitment to the idea that knowledge is
based on sensuously experienced facts (posita)
with the French Enlightenment faith in reason
and progress. The foundation of his philosophy
was “The Law of Three Stages,” which explained
how all thought evolved through a theological
stage of ﬁctitious thinking, which views all things
as animated by a will; to a metaphysical stage
of abstract thinking, in which abstract concepts
like force, substance, or spirit replace personal
wills as the principles of explanation; arriving
ﬁnally at a scientiﬁc stage of positive thinking,
which, through observation and experimenta-
tion, explains individual phenomena in terms of
general facts or laws, the number of which dimin-
ish as the science progresses.
The second half of the nineteenth century saw
French philosophy responding in various ways
to Maine de Biran’s “spiritualism,” Comte’s
positivism, and German, particularly Kantian,
idealism. Four ﬁgures stand out during these
years. Félix Ravaisson (1813–1900) brought psy-
chological insights from Biran together with a
philosophy of nature drawn from Schelling’s
metaphysics that profoundly inﬂuenced both
Catholic philosophy and the development of
personalism
in
France.
Charles
Renouvier
(1815–1903) was a critic of Hegelianism whose
neo-critical
idealism
(a
position
he
called
Criticisme) played a major role in the development
of French neo-Kantianism. Late in his life, he
moved toward a more Leibnizian metaphysical
position, and his emphasis on liberty and reﬂec-
tive consciousness led him to formulate several
of the premises of personalism. Jules Lachelier
(1832–1918) was a critic of both empiricism
and Comtean positivism. Lachelier’s idealism
was grounded in a theory of induction that
sought to resist the challenges of skepticism.
Émile Boutroux (1845–1921) was a specialist in
Leibniz and seventeenth-century German philos-
ophy but also drew on resources in French spiri-
tualism and the natural sciences as he sought to
reconcile the tensions between metaphysics and
science. His work anticipated and inﬂuenced
both Bergson and Bachelard, and it remained
inﬂuential into the ﬁrst two decades of the twen-
tieth century. Beyond these four, other French
philosophers deserving mention, in terms of
either their own work or their inﬂuence, include
Antoine
Augustin
Cournot
(1801–77),
who
insisted that chance was a real feature of the
world which needed to be handled by appropri-
ate mathematical instruments, rather than being
merely a sign of limited knowledge, as Laplace
(1749–1827) had claimed; the naturalist and
positivist historian and philosopher Hippolyte
Taine (1828–93); and Paul Janet (1823–99),
who wrote widely on ethics and politics.
The twentieth century: positivism, neo-
Kantianism, spiritualism. In the early decades
of the twentieth century, philosophy in France was
dominated by three ﬁgures – Émile Durkheim
(1858–1917),
Léon
Brunschvicg
(1869–1944),
and Henri Bergson (1859–1941) – who carried on
the positivist, idealist, and spiritualist traditions
respectively. The founder of the “French school”
of sociology, Durkheim taught philosophy at
the Sorbonne and his courses, with their mixture
390
French philosophy
French philosophy
of positivism, rationalism, and an attentiveness
to empirical detail, had a profound inﬂuence on
philosophy students. (This inﬂuence was contin-
ued by his nephew, Marcel Mauss [1878–1950],
whose Essay on the Gift [1925] was engaged by
Sartre, Bataille, Bourdieu, and Derrida, among
others.) Brunschvicg was the most important
representative of twentieth-century French neo-
Kantianism, and during his thirty years at the
Sorbonne, he produced a large body of work,
including
three
large
historical
studies
that
chronicle the increasing sophistication with which
the mind comes to understand itself and its
experience in the realms of mathematics, causality,
morality, and religion. Bergson, through a series
of major works as well as his lectures at the
Collège de France, had an enormous inﬂuence on
the philosophy of his day. Bergson’s philosophy
challenged the dominant metaphysical tradition’s
privileging of being over becoming and the
orthodox understanding of time as an endless
series of discrete and singular moments. Instead,
he suggested we understand time as we experience
it, as durée, or duration, whose moments are
themselves linked by a dynamic force he called
élan vital (vital impulse). The center of Bergson’s
vitalism,
élan
vital
allowed
him
to
account
for the evolutionary process of becoming while
avoiding
the
unsatisfactory
explanations
of
evolutionary change found in both mechanism
and ﬁnalism. Other prominent philosophers during
these years included the idealist historian of
philosophy
and
close
friend
of
Durkheim
Octave Hamelin (1856–1907); Maurice Blondel
(1861–1949), a leading Christian philosopher
working outside the Thomist tradition; and Émile
Chartier (“Alain,” 1868–1951), a beloved teacher
at the Lycée Henri-IV, whose more than 5,000
short essays (“Propos”) on ethics, aesthetics, and
politics reached a broad audience outside the
academy.
Phenomenology, existentialism, épistémo-
logie. The third and fourth decades of the twen-
tieth century saw signiﬁcant changes in French
philosophy, as the introduction of German
phenomenology
–
ﬁrst
in
the
presence
of
Max Scheler (1874–1928) and Husserlian phe-
nomenology and then in the renaissance of
Hegel studies in France – quickly displaced both
neo-Kantianism and spiritualism. As Jean Wahl
(1888–1974) argued in his inﬂuential Vers le
concret (1932), phenomenology facilitated a turn
away from idealism and spiritualism and “toward
the concrete.” This turn manifested itself ﬁrst
in the phenomenological studies of Jean-Paul
Sartre (1905–80) on the emotions and imagina-
tion, the studies of Maurice Merleau-Ponty
(1908–61) on behavior and experience, and
those
of
Emmanuel
Levinas
(1906–95)
on
consciousness and intersubjectivity. This was fol-
lowed in the 1940s by French phenomenology’s
becoming
more
existential,
marked
by
the
publications of Sartre’s Being and Nothingness
(1943) and Merleau-Ponty’s Phenomenology of
Perception (1945), as well as two important
works by Simone de Beauvoir (1908–86): The
Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) and The Second Sex
(1949). The phenomenological tradition was
also continued in the ﬁeld of aesthetics in the
work of Mikel Dufrenne (1910–95).
Two other thinkers must be mentioned in
relation to French existentialism: Catholic philos-
opher
Gabriel
Marcel
(1889–1973),
whose
Metaphysical Journal was published in 1927, and
Albert Camus (1913–60), whose essays and ﬁc-
tion were readily identiﬁed with existentialist
philosophy. While the existentialists vary from
theologically committed to aggressively atheistic,
they share a desire to examine and understand
the different components of what it means to be
human: for Marcel, the dominant themes are
embodiment and freedom; for Sartre, freedom,
facticity, and being-with-others; for Merleau-
Ponty, embodiment, temporality, perception,
and intersubjectivity; for Beauvoir, gendered
embodiment, freedom, and ethics; for Camus,
despair, alienation, and solidarity.
Three other philosophical directions in France
during the 1930s and 1940s are also deserving of
mention. Outside the universities, Catholic philos-
ophy emerges as a philosophical presence in the
work of Thomists like Pierre Teilhard de Chardin
(1881–1955), Jacques Maritain (1882–1973), and
Étienne Gilson (1884–1978), and non-Thomists
like Gabriel Marcel (1889–1973) and Emmanuel
Mounier (1905–50), as their interest in questions
concerning human existence both attracted a wide
audience and would play a signiﬁcant role in
the
development
of
existentialism.
Maritain,
e.g., called his brand of Thomism “Existentialist
Intellectualism,” while Marcel’s major philosoph-
ical work, Being and Having, which explores
such existential themes as being-in-the-world,
facticity, embodiment, and freedom, was pub-
lished in 1935, eight years before Sartre’s Being
and Nothingness. Emmanuel Mounier, another
proto-existentialist
thinker,
brought
together
Catholic spiritualism with socialist materialism
and became one of the leading spokespersons for
personalism, a philosophical position that drew
upon ideas from the earlier French spiritualists
391
French philosophy
French philosophy
and that attracted, among others, the young
Merleau-Ponty and Paul Ricoeur.
The introduction of Husserlian phenomenol-
ogy was quickly followed by a renewal of interest
in
Hegel’s
philosophy,
in
particular
The
Phenomenology of Spirit. Jean Wahl’s La Malheur
de la conscience dans la philosophie de Hegel
(1929; “The Unhappy Consciousness in Hegel’s
Philosophy”) offers a reading of Hegel that is
more “existential” and less focused on the
System.
Shortly
thereafter,
Russian
émigrés
Alexandre
Koyré
(1892–1964)
and
then
Alexandre
Kojève
(1902–68)
lectured
on
Hegel at the École Pratique des Haute Études.
Kojève’s
seminar
in
particular
emphasized
Hegel’s existential and political import as the pre-
cursor to Marx, highlighting a materialist reading
of the master-slave dialectic that demonstrates
that the future belongs to the slave – the prole-
tarian, who will emancipate himself through his
labor. Kojève’s seminar, which ran from 1933 to
1939, attracted an audience that included
several individuals who would dominate the
French intellectual scene for much of the
twentieth century, including, among others,
Raymond
Aron
(1905–83),
Georges
Bataille
(1897–1962), André Breton (1896–1966), Aron
Gurwitsch (1901–73), Jacques Lacan (1901–81),
and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. The third major ﬁg-
ure in the French Hegel renaissance was Jean
Hyppolite (1907–68), who published his French
translation of Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit in
two parts between 1939 and 1941, following this
with
his
monumental
commentary
on
the
Phenomenology – Genesis and Structure of Hegel’s
Phenomenology of Spirit – in 1946.
Michel Foucault, in discussing the origins of
contemporary French philosophy, distinguished
between a philosophy of the subject and a
philosophy of the concept, between a tradition
that attends to reﬂexivity, experience, and con-
sciousness, and one associated with formalism,
intuitionism, and the theory of science. Thus
far, only the former has been mentioned. The
latter follows the work of Gaston Bachelard
(1884–1962), Jean Cavaillès (1903–44), and
Georges Canguilhem (1904–95), and can itself
be traced to Henri Poincaré (1854–1912), Louis
Couturat (1868–1914), and Auguste Comte.
This tradition, which the French refer to as
épistémologie, attends less to the problems of
classical metaphysics than to the physical and
natural sciences. Bachelard, who taught history
and philosophy of science for many years at the
Sorbonne, published more than twenty books,
primarily on the philosophy of modern science
and the poetic and artistic imagination. He is best
known for introducing the idea of discontinuity
into the history of science. Cavaillès had strong
interests in mathematics and set theory, editing
the
correspondence
between
Cantor
and
Dedekind, and his writings and teaching on the
structure, logic, and theory of science had a
strong inﬂuence on his students Jean-Toussaint
Desanti (1914–2002), Jules Vuillemin (1920–
2001), Gilles-Gaston Granger (1920–), as well
as Louis Althusser and Foucault. Canguilhem,
who like Bachelard taught philosophy of science
at the Sorbonne for many years, was a specialist
in the biological and medical sciences, and his
groundbreaking work, On the Normal and the
Pathological (1943), was among the ﬁrst to intro-
duce normative questions into the history and
philosophy of science. Two other inﬂuential
French thinkers in philosophy of science should
be mentioned: René Thom (1923–2002), a
mathematician who worked in topology and
catastrophe
theory,
and
Gilbert
Simondon
(1924–89), whose theory of individuation had
a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on Deleuze’s philosophy.
Note should also be taken of the strong French
tradition in the history of philosophy. Major
ﬁgures here include historians of ancient philos-
ophy Émile Bréhier (1876–1952), Pierre Hadot
(1922–2010), and Pierre Aubenque (1929–);
historians
of
medieval
philosophy
Étienne
Gilson (1884–1978) and Maurice Patronnier de
Gandillac (1906–2006); historians of modern
philosophy
Henri
Gouhier
(1898–1994),
Ferdinand
Alquié
(1906–85),
and
Martial
Guéroult (1891–1976); and historical generalist
François Châtelet (1925–85).
Finally,
although
somewhat
outside
the
main trends during this period, two other inﬂu-
ential philosophers must be noted: Vladimir
Jankélévitch (1903–85), whose Traité des vertus
(1949; “Treatise on the Virtues”) was one of
the most important works of ethics and moral
psychology to appear in France in the twentieth
century; and Jean Beaufret (1907–82), a lead-
ing interpreter and disseminator (primarily
through teaching and lecturing) of Heidegger’s
thought in France.
Structuralism and poststructuralism. In
the late 1950s and early 1960s, a signiﬁcant new
philosophical transformation took place with the
emergence of structuralism as a dominant intel-
lectual paradigm. Drawing upon the four binary
oppositions central to Saussurean linguistics –
signiﬁer (signiﬁant) and signiﬁed (signiﬁé), langue
and parole, synchronic and diachronic, infrastructure
392
French philosophy
French philosophy
and superstructure – and privileging in their anal-
yses the former term in each binary pair, the
dominant structuralist thinkers – Claude Lévi-
Strauss (1908–2009), Jacques Lacan, Roland
Barthes (1915–80), Louis Althusser (1918–90) –
were able to develop anthropological, psycho-
analytic, literary, and Marxist theories that
diminished the role of the individual subject or
agent while highlighting the underlying relations
that govern social and psychic practices. But it
is also worth noting that by 1960 Merleau-
Ponty
was
lecturing
and
publishing
essays
on Saussure, linguistics, sociology, Lévi-Strauss,
and Sartre, who remained the dominant pres-
ence in existentialist philosophy; and had pub-
lished a major Marxist work, The Critique of
Dialectical Reason, which he himself described as
a “structural, historical anthropology.” While all
of the structuralists had signiﬁcant inﬂuence on
philosophy in France in the 1960s and after, the
two most philosophically inﬂuential structuralists
are Lacan and Althusser.
Lacan began his public seminars, which he
continued for twenty-six years, in 1953. These
were attended by many leading French philoso-
phers,
including,
among
others,
Althusser,
Badiou, Derrida, Foucault, Hyppolite, Merleau-
Ponty, and Ricoeur. His introduction of the
“mirror stage,” use of Saussurean linguistics to
argue that the unconscious is structured like a
language, and introduction of the thematics of
the Symbolic, the Imaginary, and the Real in his
reinterpretation of Freudian theory informed
much in French philosophy in the last four de-
cades of the twentieth century.
Althusser’s structuralist reading of Marx as
a scientist rather than humanist, which was
strongly inﬂuenced by the work of Cavaillès and
Canguilhem, put him at odds with Sartre’s exis-
tentialist reading, while the sharp distinction
he drew between ideology and science, between
the early Hegelian Marx and the later, scientiﬁc
Marx of the Grundrisse and Capital, informed the
way generations of his students at the École
Normale, where he taught from 1954 to 1980,
came to understand Marx. Also noteworthy is his
lifelong engagement with Spinoza, which played
a signiﬁcant role in the renaissance of Spinoza
scholarship in France in and after the 1960s.
While the philosophical positions that appear
in the decades following the highpoint of struc-
turalism are often seen together as “poststructur-
alism,” diverse philosophical thinking falls under
that heading. Foremost are the philosophical
contributions of Foucault, Deleuze, and Derrida,
each of whom produced a major body of work
that has signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced subsequent phi-
losophers in France and elsewhere. Foucault’s
archeological works on the history of reason
and the construction of knowledge (The History
of Madness, 1961; The Order of Things, 1966;
The Archeology of Knowledge, 1969), genealogical
investigations
of
power
and
the
subject
(Discipline and Punish, 1975; The History of
Sexuality, Vol. 1, 1976), and ethical inquiries
into the care of the self, as well as his lectures
at the Collège de France and numerous inter-
views and essays, were a dominant feature of
French intellectual life from the 1960s to his
untimely death in 1984. Deleuze and Derrida
both played major roles in the association
of French philosophy with the philosophy of
difference: Deleuze through his historical mono-
graphs on Hume, Nietzsche, Spinoza, Bergson,
and Kant, his collaborations with Félix Guattari,
his writings on art, literature, and cinema, along
with his major works Difference and Repetition
and The Logic of Sense; Derrida with his decon-
struction of the binary, oppositional thinking
that has been at the foundation of much of the
history of metaphysics.
The philosophy of difference in France also
focused
on
sexual
difference,
and
feminist
philosophy
in
the
works
of
Luce
Irigaray
(b.1930), Julia Kristeva (b.1941), and Hélène
Cixous (b.1937) differed greatly from the earlier
feminist philosophy of Beauvoir. Psychoanalysis
was another major inﬂuence on these feminist
thinkers, as it was for the structural epistemolo-
gists associated with the journal Cahiers pour
l’analyse, e.g. Jean-Claude Milner (b.1941) and
Jacques-Alain Miller (b.1944).
Three other major thinkers who came to prom-
inence in the 1960s and whose careers spanned
the late twentieth into the twenty-ﬁrst century
deserve mention. Ricoeur, who along with
Levinas and Merleau-Ponty played a major role
in introducing Husserl and then Heidegger into
French philosophy, wrote important works deal-
ing with phenomenology, hermeneutics, reli-
gion, the will, ethics, and temporality. Perhaps
most signiﬁcantly, Ricoeur worked to mediate
between competing positions, seeking points of
afﬁnity between structuralism and poststructur-
alism, and between Gadamerian hermeneutics,
Derridean
deconstruction,
and
Habermasian
critical theory.
Jean-François Lyotard (1924–98) is without
question the French philosopher most closely
associated with postmodernism, and his deﬁni-
tion of the postmodern as an “incredulity toward
metanarratives”
remains
perhaps
the
most
393
French philosophy
French philosophy
widely cited. Lyotard also wrote widely on
politics, and early in his career he was afﬁliated
with Claude Lefort (1924–2010) and Cornelius
Castoriadis’s (1922–97) political organization
and journal Socialisme ou barbarie, perhaps the
most inﬂuential Marxist group in France not
aligned with the Communists. Lyotard’s other
major interest was art and aesthetic theory,
from
his
ﬁrst
major
work,
Discourse/Figure
(1971), through his later essays and contributions
to exhibition catalogs.
The third important ﬁgure here is Michel
Serres (b.1930), who differs from his major
contemporaries in part because of his interests
in science and mathematics as well as his willing-
ness to locate sources of knowledge outside both
philosophy and science. Comprising more than
forty books, Serres’s eclectic oeuvre includes
works on Lucretius, Leibniz, Zola, physics, ther-
modynamics, angels, the senses, the history of
science, space and time, Jules Verne, and various
explorations of the communication between
science and the arts.
While the preceding thinkers continued to
produce important works in the closing decades
of the twentieth century, other important philo-
sophical voices appeared. Three who are associ-
ated to different degrees with Derrida and
deconstruction, and who produced large bodies
of work in their own right, are Sarah Kofman
(1934–94), Philippe Lacoue-Labarthe (1940–
2007), and Jean-Luc Nancy (b.1940). Several
others can be grouped around Spinozism, partic-
ularly Marxian Spinozism. Inspired in part by
the work of Deleuze and Althusser, as well as
earlier Spinoza scholars like Martial Guéroult
(1891–1976) and Ferdinand Alquié (1906–85),
signiﬁcant
ﬁgures
here
include
Alexandre
Matheron (b.1926), Pierre Macherey (b.1938),
Étienne Balibar (b.1942), and Pierre-François
Moreau (b.1948). Others, working out of a phe-
nomenology of religion and inﬂuenced by Paul
Ricoeur and Emmanuel Levinas, include Michel
Henry (1922–2002), Jean-Luc Marion (b.1946),
and Jean-Louis Chrétien (b.1952). And neo-
Kantianism is still active in France: in epistemol-
ogy, philosophy of mathematics, and philosophy
of physics one might mention the work of Jean
Petitot (b.1944); Alexis Philonenko (b.1932) in
the history of philosophy; and Alain Renaut
(b.1948) in moral and political philosophy as
well as education.
Also worth noting is that philosophy in the
Anglo-American
tradition
is
not
absent
in
France. In fact, since Merleau-Ponty’s death in
1961, in addition to Jean Hyppolite and Michel
Foucault, the prestigious chairs in philosophy at
the Collège de France have been held by analytic
historian of philosophy Jules Vuillemin, compa-
rative
epistemologist
Gilles-Gaston
Granger,
philosopher of language, Wittgenstein scholar,
and champion of analytic philosophy Jacques
Bouveresse (b.1940), philosopher of the biolog-
ical and medical sciences Anne Fagot-Largeault
(b.1938), and Canadian philosopher and histor-
ian of scientiﬁc concepts Ian Hacking (b.1936).
Other signiﬁcant ﬁgures in this tradition include
epistemologist and philosopher of mathematics
Jean Petitot (b.1944) and philosophers of lan-
guage and mind Vincent Descombes (b.1943)
and Pascal Engel (b.1954).
Finally, three other ﬁgures deserve mention,
each having only recently attracted attention
outside France. Alain Badiou (b.1937) was
among the students who worked with Althusser
in the 1960s, and he has remained committed to
leftist political projects throughout his career,
drawing upon set theory and Lacanian psycho-
analysis. His major works, Being and Event (1988)
and Logics of Worlds: Being and Event, Vol. 2 (2006),
are perhaps the most signiﬁcant works in ontol-
ogy written in France since Sartre’s Being and
Nothingness. Jacques Rancière (b.1940) was also
afﬁliated with Althusser in the 1960s, and has
written extensively over the past ﬁve decades
on topics related to politics, ideology, and aes-
thetics. François Laruelle (b.1937), whose earlier
work responds to Nietzsche, Heidegger, Derrida,
and Deleuze, has given way to a radically new
position he calls “non-philosophy” (with the
“non” functioning as it does in “non-Euclidean
geometry”), which operates from a perspective
in which thinking is not representative of, but
radically immanent to, the Real.
