generative grammar. See GRAMMAR, PHILOSO-
PHY OF LANGUAGE.
generic consistency, principle of. See UNIVER-
SALIZABILITY.
generics, statements such as ‘Tigers are striped’,
‘A duck lays eggs’, ‘The dodo is extinct’, and
‘Ticks carry Lyme disease’. Like quantiﬁed state-
ments (e.g., ‘All tigers are striped’, ‘Most ravens
are black’), generics express generalizations.
However, unlike quantiﬁed statements, generics
do not tell us how many members of the category
have
the
property.
For
example,
if
asked,
‘How many ravens are black?’ one could reply,
‘All [/some/most] ravens are black’, but one
cannot
felicitously
reply
with
the
generic
‘Ravens are black’.
In English, generics take three syntactic forms:
bare plural (e.g., ‘Tigers are striped’), indeﬁnite
singular (e.g., ‘A tiger is striped’), and deﬁnite sin-
gular (e.g., ‘The tiger is striped’). All three forms
can be used to express generalizations concerning
individuals – the three versions of ‘Tigers are
striped’ all indicate something about the proper-
ties of individual tigers. The bare plural and the
deﬁnite singular can also express claims about
kinds: e.g., one could say, ‘Tigers are extinct’
or ‘The tiger is extinct’, where ‘is extinct’ is a
property that can be had only by a kind, not an
individual. However, indeﬁnite singulars cannot
be used in this way: ‘A tiger is extinct’ is not an
acceptable sentence.
It is difﬁcult to provide a formal truth-
conditional
analysis
of
generics.
Why
does
‘Ducks lay eggs’ strike us as true, while ‘Ducks
are female’ does not? There are more female
ducks than egg-laying ducks, since some female
ducks
are
infertile
or
immature.
Why
is
‘Mosquitoes carry malaria’ true when just 1 per-
cent of mosquitoes have the property, while
‘Books are paperbacks’ is false, despite more
than 80 percent of books being paperbacks?
Some
theorists
have
recently
argued
that
generics are best studied from the perspective of
empirical psychology rather than that of formal
semantics.
See also QUANTIFICATION.
S.-J.L.
generic sentence. See PHILOSOPHY OF LANGUAGE.
genetic epistemology. See PIAGET.
genetic fallacy. See INFORMAL FALLACY.
genotext. See KRISTEVA.
Gentile, Giovanni (1875–1944), Italian idealist
philosopher and educational reformer. He taught
at the universities of Palermo, Pisa, and Rome,
and became minister of education in the ﬁrst
years of Mussolini’s government (1922–24). He
was the most inﬂuential intellectual of the Fascist
regime and promoted a radical transformation of
the Italian school system, most of which did not
survive that era. Gentile rejected Hegel’s dialec-
tics as the process of an objectiﬁed thought. His
actualism (or actual idealism) claims that only the
pure act of thinking or the Transcendental
Subject can undergo a dialectical process. All real-
ity, such as nature, God, good, and evil, is imma-
nent in the dialectics of the Transcendental
Subject,
which
is
distinct
from
Empirical
Subjects. Among his major works are La teoria
generale dello spirito come atto puro (1916; trans-
lated as The Theory of Mind as Pure Act, 1922) and
Sistema di logica come teoria del conoscere (“System of
Logic as a Theory of Knowledge,” 1917).
Gentile’s pedagogical views were also inﬂu-
enced by actualism. Education overcomes the
difﬁculties of intersubjective communication
and realizes the unity of the pupil and the
teacher
within
the
Transcendental
Subject
(Sommario di pedagogia come scienza ﬁlosoﬁca,
“Summary
of
Pedagogy
as
a
Philosophical
Science,” 1913–14). Actualism was inﬂuential
in Italy during Gentile’s life. With Croce’s
historicism, it inﬂuenced British idealists like
Bosanquet and Collingwood.
See also IDEALISM, ITALIAN PHILOSOPHY.
P.Gar.
408
generalization argument
Gentile, Giovanni
genus. See DEFINITION.
genus, summum. See GENUS GENERALISSIMUM.
genus
generalissimum
(Latin,
‘most
general
genus’), a genus that is not a species of some
higher genus; a broadest natural kind. One of
the ten Aristotelian categories, it is also called
summum genus (highest genus). For Aristotle and
many of his followers, the ten categories are not
species of some higher all-inclusive genus – say,
being. Otherwise, that all-inclusive genus would
wholly include its differences, and would be
universally predicable of them. But no genus is
predicable of its differences in this manner. Few
authors explained this reasoning clearly, but
some pointed out that if the difference ‘rational’
just meant ‘rational animal’, then to deﬁne ‘man’
as ‘rational animal’ would be to deﬁne him as
‘rational animal animal’, which is ill formed.
So too generally: no genus can include its differ-
ences in this way. Thus there is no all-inclusive
genus; the ten categories are the most general
genera. See also DEFINITION, PRAEDICAMENTA,
PREDICABLES.
P.V.S.
geometrical method. See SPINOZA.
geometrical order. See SPINOZA.
geometric conventionalism. See POINCARÉ.
geometry, Euclidean. See EUCLIDEAN GEOME-
TRY.
geometry, non-Euclidean. See NON-EUCLIDEAN
GEOMETRY.
German idealism. See GERMAN PHILOSOPHY.
German philosophy, the philosophy produced
either in the German language or in other
languages by certain authors who at least occa-
sionally wrote in German. While including the
work of Austrian, German Swiss, and even
Eastern European thinkers, such as György
Lukács
(1885–1971), who wrote mostly in
German, this deﬁnition excludes, e.g., the work
of Albertus Magnus (c.1206–80), who wrote only
in Latin and whose education and impact were,
as with most medieval thinkers, European, even
if he happened to live in the Germany of today.
(Territorial
deﬁnitions
of
what
constitutes
German philosophy would be problematic for
various reasons, among which are the shifting
borders of Germany.) From the fourteenth to
the nineteenth century, most philosophers who
wrote in German published also in Latin – in the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries sometimes
also in French when addressing a non-academic
European audience; and it does not make sense
to regard only the relatively few German texts by
Leibniz, but not his Latin and French ones, as
belonging to German philosophy.
The ﬁrst German philosopher who deliber-
ately wrote also in the vernacular (Middle
High German) and by doing so created a
distinct German tradition was Meister Eckhart
(c.1260–1327). His philosophical mysticism,
rooted in a rationalist interpretation of theology
and strongly insisting on the union of God and
the
human
soul,
was
condemned
by
the
Catholic Church but inspired many German
thinkers up to Hegel. Cardinal Nicholas of
Cusa (1401–64) was accused of proximity to
Eckhart, although this did not derail his spec-
tacular ecclesiastical career. Cusanus’s episte-
mology focused on the difference between
reason and intellect; his philosophy of nature
broke with Aristotelianism and anticipated
Copernicus and Bruno; his political philosophy
tackled that unique political structure, the Holy
Roman Empire, which later also fascinated
Pufendorf (1632–94) and Hegel; his theology
insisted on interreligious dialogue and the
importance of justiﬁcation through faith.
The last point was crucial for Martin Luther
(1483–1546), who, though not a philosopher
and even opposed to any attempt to justify
Christianity
philosophically,
shaped
German
(and Scandinavian) culture as probably no other
ﬁgure has and thus could not help inﬂuencing
German (and Scandinavian) philosophy. First, he
made New High German an astonishingly rich
language, which could be used by philosophers
such as Paracelsus (1493–1541), who, at the
University of Basel, was the ﬁrst to lecture in
German.
(The
general
shift
from
Latin
to
German at the universities occurred only in the
eighteenth century.) Second, by his rejection of
Aquinas, he unwittingly triggered the develop-
ment of a truly original philosophy, no longer
fettered by Scholasticism, as philosophical tradi-
tions usually were in Catholic countries. Third,
Luther’s focus on the original text of the Bible
led to an extraordinary hermeneutical sensibility
in German elites; the combination of philosophy
and
philology
became
a
common
concern
for most German philosophers. Many of them
knew
Greek
well;
some,
e.g.
Hegel
and
Schelling, also learned Hebrew. Fourth, the polit-
ical revolt of the Protestant princes against the
409
genus
German philosophy
Empire led to the creation of state universities in
the many semiautonomous principalities within
the Empire; and although the Empire established
its ﬁrst university much later than most European
countries (in the late fourteenth century), in the
seventeenth century it had forty universities,
while England made do with only Oxford and
Cambridge. From the eighteenth century on,
the majority of German philosophers were linked
to universities. Luther’s ﬁfth contribution was the
most dangerous: the price that Luther paid for the
princes’ support was his absolute loyalty to them,
and his resolute denial of any right of resistance
had a strong impact on later German political
philosophy, which did not elaborate a theory of
resistance comparable to that of Locke. (The
political philosopher and defender of the Dutch
Revolt, Johannes Althusius [c.1563–1638], was
not a Lutheran, but a Calvinist.) A crucial ﬁgure
of early Lutheran thought was Jakob Böhme
(1575–1624), a “naive” philosopher who was
pursued by the Lutheran Church authorities
because of his innovative ideas afﬁrming the
presence of a negative principle within God him-
self. His books attracted numerous international
followers in Protestant countries; when Henry
More censured “Teutonic philosophy,” he had
“Behmenism” in mind.
Doubtless the greatest German philosopher of
the seventeenth century was Gottfried Wilhelm
Leibniz (1646–1716). Even though it was only his
admirer Christian Wolff (1679–1754), and not he
himself, who published most of his books in
German, these became the basis of the Leibniz-
Wolfﬁan philosophy that dominated eighteenth-
century
philosophical
training
in
Germany.
Leibniz himself actively promoted the use of
German as an academic language, and he con-
tributed to the ﬁrst academic journal in Germany,
the Acta Eruditorum (founded in 1682); and, in
addition to being a member of various foreign
academies, he became the ﬁrst president of the
Brandenburg (later, the Prussian) Academy of
Sciences.
Leibniz
tried
to
synthesize
the
Scholastic tradition with early modern science,
to which his contributions were enormous; he
thereby created a distinctive German commit-
ment to science and religion at the same time.
(Nietzsche’s revolt against religion in the nine-
teenth century, therefore, had to be connected
with a revolt against reason.) Leibniz elaborated
the most complex rational theology of modernity
and based it on various proofs of God, such as the
ontological proof. While inﬂuenced by Spinoza’s
attempt at developing a metaphysics of natural
laws, Leibniz insisted on the contingency of
natural laws. Still, they are not the result of an
ungrounded divine decision, as they are in
Descartes’s voluntarism, but are rooted in the
desire of God to create “the best possible
world.” This doctrine is new not because it pre-
supposes that God’s will is bound by axiological
criteria, but because by linking the existence of
God to the creation of the best possible world –
unlike Aquinas – Leibniz rendered the question
of theodicy far more difﬁcult: it would sufﬁce to
show that the actual world does not have max-
imal value to disprove the existence of God. His
doctrine strengthened the hope of German
philosophers that humans may discover truths
about the world by a priori speculation (even if
Leibniz himself distinguished between truths of
reason and truths of fact). The ultimate elements
of
the
world
are
subjective
centers
called
“monads.” This is a form of idealism, but differ-
ent from idealisms in the ﬁrst person (such as
solipsism). A feature of his philosophy that
increasingly
vexed
the
eighteenth-century
German
philosophers
was his determinism,
which follows from his acceptance of the princi-
ple of sufﬁcient reason.
Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) began his career
as a follower of Leibniz and Wolff. Partly
because of Rousseau’s dissatisfaction with the
Enlightenment, and partly because of Hume’s
criticism of our concept of causality, Kant refor-
mulated his position in a critical philosophy that
became the greatest watershed in the history of
German philosophy. A concern with the founda-
tion of science, as well as with the speciﬁc pietistic
form of Lutheranism that had replaced tradi-
tional orthodoxy by focusing on an internal
appropriation of the Gospel, were the two pillars
of Kant’s philosophy, which achieved its mature
articulation in the three Critiques and his positive
metaphysical works on nature and ethics. His
basic contributions to German philosophy and
to German culture in general include the straight-
forward rejection of the rationalist program of
proofs of the existence of God and the immortal-
ity of the soul. (Hume’s Dialogues, on the other
hand, were composed in such a subtle manner as
to deceive many readers of the nineteenth cen-
tury, who in England, but no longer in Germany,
still cherished the argument from design.) At the
same time, Kant replaced the theoretical argu-
ments for God and immortality by practical
postulates, whose epistemic status is not easy to
ascertain. Kant did not ground ethics, which he
conceived as autonomous, in religion; instead,
he held that only faith in a moral principle under-
lying nature can sustain our conviction that
410
German philosophy
German philosophy
morality has a chance to operate successfully,
given that morality itself does not stem from
nature.
In practical philosophy, Kant broke with an
ancient tradition of eudaimonism; he taught
that the morality of an intention is irreducible to
its contribution to one’s own happiness. (This is
compatible with human beings’ having a duty to
promote the happiness of other people.) Through
his ethico-theology, Kant gave a peculiar reli-
gious ﬂavor to the universalist and formalist
ethics that had been elaborated throughout the
Enlightenment, in many European countries
often in the context of a struggle against ofﬁcial
Christianity, allied as it was to the ancien régime. A
well-known problem for Kant’s formalism is that
he apparently could not justify exceptions to
prima facie norms, such as not to lie or not to
resist state power. His transcendental idealism
claimed to render, as paradoxical as it sounds,
compatibilism and incompatibilism compatible –
the principle of causality is a priori valid and a
necessary
presupposition
of
experience
and
empirical science, but it originates in the sponta-
neity of our understanding and applies only to
the phenomenal world. The true, noumenal real-
ity (the things-in-themselves) may well have
space for libertarian freedom.
Kant also taught that the stream of conscious-
ness manifests only the phenomenal, not the
real self, thus preparing the German interest in
an
unconscious
ground
of
the
self
from
Schopenhauer to Freud. For technical philoso-
phy, probably his most original insight concerns
the problem of synthetic a priori propositions,
which, according to him, underlie mathematics,
pure science, and ethics. Despite this modiﬁca-
tion of empiricism, Kant’s theoretical philosophy
was more oriented toward empiricism than
all German philosophy before and much of it
after him, and his principle of signiﬁcance for
theoretical reason prepares the way for logical
positivism.
The
desire
to
overcome
Kant’s
dualism
between
phenomena
and
noumena,
which
was widely perceived to be a performatively
contradictory doctrine, was one of the roots of
the movement that in its very name seems to
express a particular afﬁnity to the German spirit:
German idealism. Its other root was a new
approach toward human culture, art, and his-
tory, partly because of an appropriation of
Greek culture, as in the history of ancient art
by Johann Joachim Winckelmann (1717–68),
partly because of dissatisfaction with the paro-
chialism of Lutheran orthodoxy, even if most of
the
new
movement’s
supporters,
beginning
with Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–81), were
trained as theologians, and its leader, Johann
Gottfried Herder (1744–1803), even became a
Lutheran
superintendent
who
transformed
Protestantism. This turn toward history was
connected, thanks to the fateful encounter in
1770 between Herder and Johann Wolfgang
Goethe (1749–1832), to the rise of a new form
of German poetry, which is generally regarded as
the peak of German literature (while the other
great European literatures, with the exception
of that of Russia, peaked much earlier). The
expressive power of the new poetry inspired
German thought, and the latter made German
literature more reﬂective than other national
literatures. A student of Kant, Herder was also
profoundly
inﬂuenced
by
Johann
Georg
Hamann (1730–88). One of the ﬁrst critics of
Kant’s ﬁrst Critique, Hamann defended an evan-
gelical Christianity focusing on God’s word as
manifest in the Bible, but also in the whole of
human history, and he deliberately rejected, in
the name of the immediacy of belief, all attempts
at a rational foundation of religion. This rejection
became important both for Friedrich Heinrich
Jacobi (1743–1819) and for Søren Kierkegaard
(1813–55). Although mainly a poet, Friedrich
Schiller (1759–1805) has a place in the history
of aesthetics and ethics because of his challenge
to Kant’s rigorism and his proposal of an aesthet-
ical education that would mediate between sen-
sibility and moral autonomy. A revolution in
aesthetics was achieved by the brothers August
Wilhelm Schlegel (1767–1845) and Friedrich
Schlegel (1772–1829), probably the ﬁrst to
know most works of world literature, thanks
in part to their pathbreaking study of Sanskrit.
Their early Romantic journal Athenaeum, to which
the poet-philosopher Novalis (1772–1801) and
Friedrich Daniel Ernst Schleiermacher (1768–
1834) contributed, was important not only for its
content but also for employing new literary forms,
such as dialogues and aphorisms. (Schleiermacher
is renowned mainly as a theologian, but his works
in philosophy of religion, ethics, and hermeneutics
have their place in the history of philosophy.)
A crucial idea of the time was the belief that
Germans played the role of new Greeks; and, in
its strong orientation toward the study of ancient
languages, the reform of German gymnasiums
and universities by the linguist and philosopher
of language Wilhelm von Humboldt (1767–
1835), which occurred during his time in the
Prussian Ministry of Internal Affairs, shaped
German education until the 1960s.
411
German philosophy
German philosophy
Kant’s philosophy elicited early on philosoph-
ical criticisms from Catholics, such as the former
priest Karl Leonhard Reinhold (1757–1823), and
Jews, such as the Lithuanian Salomon Maimon
(1753–1800), who was inﬂuenced by the German
version of the Jewish Enlightenment (Haskalah)
and its main representative, Lessings’s friend
Moses Mendelssohn (1729–86). But the three
classic post-Kantian philosophers were trained
as Lutheran theologians: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
(1762–1814), Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
(1775–1854), and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
(1770–1831). They all rejected the doctrine of
things-in-themselves and averred the knowability
of the ultimate ground of reality. For all of them,
the task of philosophy consisted in developing the
basic categories of reality by following a method
of concept formation often called “dialectic,”
based on the repeated integration of polar oppo-
sites. They all were committed to some form
of holism: only through a system covering all
its disciplines was a plausible foundation of phi-
losophy possible. Whereas for Fichte theoretical
philosophy, philosophy of law, ethics, and phi-
losophy of religion were the basic disciplines
leading to an ever stronger autonomy of the
self, Schelling developed a philosophy of nature
according to which the main structural elements
of nature, such as gravitation, light, and organ-
isms, were somehow analogous to the basic
structures of the mind. For him, the approach of
transcendental philosophy, from the mind to
nature, and that of natural philosophy, from
nature to the mind, were complementary enter-
prises. Furthermore, philosophy of art played a
special role in the system of the young Schelling.
But the greatest architectonic talent can be found
in Hegel’s Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences.
His most original contribution lies in the philoso-
phy of the social world, in which alone moral
behavior can be situated. Hegel’s very precise
understanding of historical processes and his
elaborate lectures on philosophy of history and
the history of philosophy have often led to his-
toricist interpretations of his thought. But his
foundational work, The Science of Logic, described
timeless structures, and his philosophy of nature
and mind claimed to grasp the essential struc-
tures of these realms in a way similar to Plato
and Aristotle. Concepts, in this view, were not
simply subjective constructions, but what under-
lies reality. Historical development was teleologi-
cally oriented toward the rise of the modern
liberal state and a philosophy based on autonomy.
One of the ﬁrst critics of Hegel, the late Schelling,
questioned the idea of a system founded on reason
alone and pointed to the irreducibility of being to
concepts. The collapse of Hegelianism had largely
to do with the enormous increase of empirical
knowledge in the nineteenth century that did
not seem to ﬁt into his system. Some of Hegel’s
ideas persisted in the more empirically inclined
metaphysics of Hermann Lotze (1817–81), who
marks the transition to a less “heroic” form of
philosophy, which addresses mainly colleagues
and begins to focus on publications in philosophy
journals.
Kant’s
subjectivist
epistemology
could
be
de-transcendentalized and read as an anthropo-
logical account. This happened to some extent in
the highly innovative philosophy of Arthur
Schopenhauer (1788–1860). He continued the
quest for the thing-in-itself, which he situated
in the will, which shows itself most strongly in
the sexual drive and on which the intellectual
functions depend. By denying the autonomy
of reason, Schopenhauer prepared the way for
the irrationalist philosophies of his successors.
However, he wanted to overcome the will in an
asceticism inspired by Hindu and Buddhist phi-
losophies, which for the ﬁrst time were experi-
enced by a European as superior alternatives
to Christian theism. His ethics rested on the
sentiment of compassion and rejected Kant’s
rationalist formalism. A peculiar combination of
Hegel and Schopenhauer was later elaborated by
Eduard von Hartmann (1842–1906).
While the Hegelian right read Hegel as an inno-
vative Lutheran theologian, the Hegelian left
was characterized by a historicist radicalization
of Hegel. Ludwig Feuerbach (1804–72) elimi-
nated the metaphysical foundations still present
in Hegel’s speculative philosophy of religion and
saw religion simply as an anthropological phe-
nomenon. Karl Marx (1818–83) connected a sar-
castic criticism of the contradictions of bourgeois
society to a philosophy of history that saw the end
of history not in liberalism, but in communism.
(This distinguished him from the otherwise
similar philosophy of August Comte.) Working
for a revolutionary transformation of society,
Marx subordinated theory to practice. Thus he
had probably the greatest political impact of all
German philosophers – not only in the Soviet
Union but also in German social democracy,
which in the early twentieth century mitigated
Marxism with neo-Kantianism. At the same
time, traditional foundational disciplines such as
epistemology played almost no role in Marx’s
philosophy.
The iconoclasm of Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–
1900) went beyond Schopenhauer (his main
412
German philosophy
German philosophy
inspiration), Feuerbach, and Marx, for he fought
not only against Christianity but also against the
universalism of modern ethics. His commitment
to a historical analysis of the genesis of values,
his subtle psychology of hidden motivations
of human behavior, and his admiration for a
Greece no longer amalgamated with Christian
values, as it had been in earlier forms of human-
ism, ﬁnally led him to a radically perspectivist
epistemology, to a metaphysics for which the
will to power is the ultimate ground of reality,
and to a doctrine of the superman who disposes
of traditional virtues. The deliberately contradic-
tory form in which he presented his thought
(mainly
in
stylistically
brilliant
aphorisms)
explains why his work has encountered diamet-
rically opposed interpretations. It cannot be
doubted that the National Socialist interpretation
could ﬁnd numerous passages in its support, even
if, after his break with Richard Wagner, Nietzsche
detested anti-Semitism and German nationalism
(which had been fomented by Fichte and peaked
after the late uniﬁcation of Germany in 1871).
After Nietzsche’s destruction of traditional
standards of rationality, three new attempts at a
regrounding of philosophy are noteworthy. The
ﬁrst was connected with Lotze’s pupil Gottlob
Frege (1848–1925), who created the modern
notation of formal logic, and whose reﬂections
on philosophy of logic, mathematics, and lan-
guage gave these disciplines a new level of pre-
cision. The combination of his logical rigor with
nineteenth- and early twentieth-century enthu-
siasm for the success of the natural sciences
led to logical positivism, which found a manifesto
in Ludwig Wittgenstein’s (1889–1951) Tractatus
Logico-Philosophicus and whose central ideas were
elaborated in the Vienna and Berlin Circles
by philosophers such as Moritz Schlick (1882–
1936), Rudolf Carnap (1891–1970), and Hans
Reichenbach (1891–1953). The two latter ﬁgures
and many other German-speaking philosophers
ﬂed from National Socialism to English-speaking
countries, often changing the language of their
publications. This should not hide the fact that
analytical philosophy in its origin was largely a
German, thus Continental, school of thought.
The second attempt to reground philosophy
was
neo-Kantianism.
The
Marburg
School
focused on logic and epistemology. Its founder,
Hermann Cohen (1848–1919), also had a strong
impact on Jewish assimilation because of his
rationalist interpretation of Judaism and his
opposition to Zionism, while the Baden School
with Wilhelm Windelband (1848–1915) and
Heinrich Rickert (1863–1936) tried to establish
a foundation for the social sciences and human-
ities, which Kant himself had neglected but which
achieved an extraordinary quality in nineteenth-
century Germany and triggered Wilhelm Dilthey’s
(1833–1911) approach to the Geisteswissenschaften
on the basis of a philosophy of life. A particularly
versatile neo-Kantian was Ernst Cassirer (1874–
1945), who both reacted to the revolution of
physics in the early twentieth century and elabo-
rated a complex philosophy of culture.
The third grounding attempt was connected
with Edmund Husserl (1859–1938), a pupil of
the
former
Catholic
priest
Franz
Brentano
(1838–1917). Brentano tried to justify a realistic
philosophy by psychological studies and an anal-
ysis of intentionality. Husserl became famous
through his refutation of psychologism in the
philosophy of logic, but developed his own phe-
nomenological position as a combination of a
neo-Cartesian
“bracketing”
of
the
external
world, a commitment to Platonic essences, and
an in-depth study of features of consciousness,
such as temporality. Later themes for him were
intersubjectivity and the relation of the life-world
to science. The foremost ethicist of the phenom-
enological school was Max Scheler (1874–1928),
whose criticism of Kant led him to a content-based
value-ethics. The greatest phenomenologist theo-
rist of the arts was Roman Ingarden (1893–1970).
Husserl’s most inﬂuential pupil was Martin
Heidegger (1889–1976). But Husserl understood
quickly that Heidegger’s Being and Time in fact
had broken with the philosophical intuitions of
the teacher to whom it was dedicated. The impor-
tance of the book consists in the weaving together
of ontological reﬂections on human existence, a
radicalization of the analysis of the temporality of
humans by focusing on mortality, a justiﬁcation
of the historical sciences inspired by Dilthey, and
a challenge to traditional ethics posed by the
reinterpretation of terms like guilt and conscience
in a completely formal way: what counts is decid-
edness (Entschlossenheit), not content. It is fair
to say that, while not yet a Nazi in 1927,
Heidegger did not have moral resources against
National Socialism, the rise of which was facili-
tated by irrationalist philosophical tendencies of
the 1920s and a feeling, widespread after the
defeat of 1918 and eloquently expressed by
Oswald Spengler (1880–1936), that Western civ-
ilization had come to an end. Heidegger joined
the Nazi party in May 1933, as did other leading
German intellectuals – the jurist and political the-
orist Carl Schmitt (1888–1985), who regarded
friend-enemy relations as the essence of politics,
and the sociologist-philosopher Arnold Gehlen
413
German philosophy
German philosophy
(1904–76), who, together with Helmuth Plessner
(1892–1985), created the typically German disci-
pline of philosophical anthropology. Politically
impeccable
was
the behavior of the other
great existentialist philosopher, Karl Jaspers
(1883–1969), whose contributions to the philos-
ophy of psychiatry remain fundamental.
German philosophy never fully recovered from
the moral and intellectual devastation caused
by Nazi rule. The philosophy of the German
Democratic Republic lacked the basic presuppo-
sition of intelligent investigation, namely political
freedom. In the Federal Republic of Germany,
philosophy after 1945 was for a long time under
the spell of Heidegger, whose late philosophy
denied individual responsibility for radical histor-
ical changes that were supposed to drive Western
civilization, from Plato to the era of modern
technology
and
totalitarianism,
away
from
original
contact
with
Being.
Of
Heidegger’s
Jewish pupils, Karl Löwith (1897–1973), Herbert
Marcuse (1898–1979), Hans Jonas (1903–93), and
Hannah Arendt (1906–75), only the ﬁrst returned
to Germany, namely to Heidelberg, where he
was the colleague of another Heidegger pupil,
Hans-Georg Gadamer (1900–2002). Gadamer’s
main ﬁeld of activity was hermeneutics, a disci-
pline dear to the German tradition since the
seventeenth century. Gadamer’s central idea
was that the justiﬁcation of interpretation is to
be found neither in the author’s intention nor in
any normative principles, but in the effectual
history connecting the interpretandum with the
interpreter. His answer, however, was not only
historicist, for Gadamer also insisted strongly on
the topic about which the interpreter wants to
learn from the interpretandum. Interpretation is
not concerned with the mental states of the
author, but with potential truth. While this
view favored a respectful attitude toward tradi-
tions, the other philosophical center of postwar
Germany, Frankfurt, supported radical change.
The leaders of the ﬁrst Frankfurt School, Max
Horkheimer (1895–1973) and Theodor Adorno
(1903–69), offered a neo-Marxian criticism of
capitalism that attacked the culture industry of
late modernity. While Horkheimer and Adorno’s
analysis of the dialectical, i.e. self-destructive,
tendencies of the modern Enlightenment remains
striking and Adorno’s writings in aesthetics offer
classical insights into the essence of modern art,
the epistemological and metaphysical foundations
of the ﬁrst Frankfurt School were opaque, if
not self-contradictory. (There is an interesting
parallelism to the late Heidegger, insofar as both
Adorno and Heidegger saw their era in the grip
of a context of deception that makes it unintelli-
gible how these philosophers could advance truth
claims.)
The second Frankfurt School, led by Karl-Otto
Apel (b.1922) and Jürgen Habermas (b.1929),
tried to give a stronger foundation to the enter-
prise of a critical theory of society by seriously
studying Anglo-American thinkers, from Peirce
to contemporary analytical philosophers. Apel
proposed an intersubjective transformation of
Kant’s transcendental philosophy and dedicated
important studies to the central issue of how basic
principles of philosophy can be ascertained. His
idea that in any rational discourse basic principles
of a universalist morality are already acknowl-
edged was connected by Habermas to a complex
theory of the social world, which challenged the
tendency to deprive the social sciences of any
normative force (a tendency forcefully articu-
lated by Max Weber [1864–1920]).
Perhaps the most inﬂuential German philoso-
pher of the 1980s was Hans Jonas. His work
on philosophical biology, written in English,
generalized
Heidegger’s
analysis
of
human
being-in-the-world to an ontology of the organic
mode of being. On this basis, he ﬁnally published,
returning to the German of his youth, an envi-
ronmental ethics that challenged many com-
monplaces of current metaethics, such as the
is-ought divide. The fact that Germany is now
one of the leading countries in environmental
policies is connected to the reception of his
thought.
There are good reasons to believe that the era
of national philosophies is coming to an end. The
rise of English as an academic lingua franca, the
mobility of modern intellectuals, and the decay of
old German traditions make it doubtful whether
there is still such a thing as a German philosophy.
But it existed in the past, and its commitment to
reason, its belief in a priori knowledge, its intel-
lectual religiosity, its love of system building, its
profound interest in history and the humanities,
its love of Greece, and the powerful presence of
philosophers in public debates were probably the
major features that gave it a speciﬁc identity.
See
also
AUSTRIAN
PHILOSOPHY,
FICHTE,
HEGEL,
KANT,
NORDIC
PHILOSOPHY,
VIENNA
CIRCLE.
V.H.
Gerson, Jean de, original name, Jean Charlier
(1363–1429), French theologian, philosopher,
and ecclesiastic. He studied in Paris, and suc-
ceeded the nominalist Pierre d’Ailly as chancellor
of the university in 1395. Both d’Ailly and Gerson
played a prominent part in the work of the
414
Gerson, Jean de
Gerson, Jean de
Council
of
Constance
(1414–18).
Much
of
Gerson’s inﬂuence on later thinkers arose from
his conciliarism, the view that the church is a
political society and that a general council, acting
on behalf of the church, has the power to depose
a pope who fails to promote the church’s welfare,
for it seemed that similar arguments could apply
to other forms of political society. Gerson’s con-
ciliarism was not constitutionalism in the modern
sense, for he appealed to corporate and hierarch-
ical ideas of church government, and did not
rest his case on any principle of individual rights.
His main writings dealt with mystical theology,
which, he thought, brings the believer closer to
the beatiﬁc vision of God than do other forms of
theology. He was inﬂuenced by St. Bonaventure
and Albertus Magnus, but especially by Pseudo-
Dionysius, whom he saw as a disciple of St. Paul
and not as a Platonist. He was thus able to adopt
an anti-Platonic position in his attacks on the
mystic Ruysbroeck and on contemporary fol-
lowers of Duns Scotus, such as Jean de Ripa.
In dismissing Scotist realism, he made use of nom-
inalist positions, particularly those that empha-
sized divine freedom. He warned theologians
against being misled by pride into supposing that
natural reason alone could solve metaphysical
problems; and he emphasized the importance of
a priest’s pastoral duties. Despite his early prom-
inence, he spent the last years of his life in relative
obscurity.
E.J.A.
Gersonides, also called Levi ben Gershom
(1288–1344), French Jewish philosopher and
mathematician, the leading Jewish Aristotelian
after Maimonides. Gersonides was also a distin-
guished
Talmudist,
Bible commentator, and
astronomer. His philosophical writings include
supercommentaries on most of Averroes’ com-
mentaries on Aristotle (1319–24); On the Correct
Syllogism (1319), a treatise on the modal syllo-
gism; and a major Scholastic treatise, The Wars of
the Lord (1317–29). In addition, his biblical
commentaries rank among the best examples of
philosophical scriptural exegesis; especially note-
worthy is his interpretation of the Song of Songs
as an allegory describing the ascent of the human
intellect to the agent intellect.
Gersonides’ mentors in the Aristotelian tradi-
tion were Maimonides and Averroes. However,
more than either of them, Gersonides held
philosophical truth and revealed truth to be coex-
tensive: he acknowledged neither the conﬂict
that Averroes saw between reason and revelation
nor Maimonides’ critical view of the limitations
of the human intellect. Furthermore, while
remaining within the Aristotelian framework,
Gersonides was not uncritical of it; his inde-
pendence can be illustrated by two of his most
distinctive positions. First, against Maimonides,
Gersonides claimed that it is possible to demon-
strate both the falsity of the Aristotelian theory of
the eternity of the world (Averroes’ position)
and the absurdity of creation ex nihilo, the tradi-
tional rabbinic view that Maimonides adopted,
though for non-demonstrative reasons. Instead
Gersonides advocated the Platonic theory of
temporal
creation
from
primordial
matter.
Second, unlike Maimonides and Averroes, who
both held that the alleged contradiction between
divine
foreknowledge
of
future
contingent
particulars and human freedom is spurious,
Gersonides took the dilemma to be real. In
defense of human freedom, he then argued
that it is logically impossible even for God to
have knowledge of particulars as particulars,
since his knowledge is only of general laws.
At the same time, by redeﬁning ‘omniscience’
as knowing everything that is knowable, he
showed that this impossibility is no deﬁciency
in God’s knowledge.
Although Gersonides’ biblical commentaries
received wide immediate acceptance, subsequent
medieval Jewish philosophers, e.g. Hasdai Crescas,
by and large reacted negatively to his rigorously
rationalistic positions. Especially with the decline
of Aristotelianism within the philosophical world,
both Jewish and Christian, he was either criticized
sharply or simply ignored.
See
also
ARISTOTLE,
AVERROES,
JEWISH
PHILOSOPHY, MAIMONIDES, PHILOSOPHY OF RELI-
GION.
J.Ste.
Gert, Bernard (1934–2011), American moral
philosopher and Hobbes scholar known for his
general theory of morality and for interpretations
of Hobbes’s ethics that challenge conventional
wisdom; also in the vanguard of philosophers
who brought the methods of analytic philosophy
to bear on issues in biomedical ethics.
Gert developed and defended a secular theory
of morality whose lineage is the modern natural
law tradition that began with Grotius. Its virtues
include clarity of exposition and ease and breadth
of application to daily life and various profes-
sions. Gert’s own application of his theory to
issues in biomedical ethics exempliﬁes the latter
virtue and helped to extend the theory’s inﬂu-
ence beyond philosophy. He ﬁrst presented the
theory in The Moral Rules (1970) and then, over
thirty-ﬁve years, revised and expanded it in new
editions. The theory gained a broad following
415
Gersonides
Gert, Bernard
throughout the world among philosophers and
others who wanted a theory, other than utilita-
rianism, that grounded morality in rationality
and impartiality and applied to the common
problems of human life. The theory’s core is a
systematic exposition of moral duties as arising
from ten basic rules. These represent a public
system of prohibitions and requirements. Their
validity consists in the endorsement that each, as
a rule in a public system, would receive from
every rational person who considered it impar-
tially. These themes bear the imprint of the
inﬂuential ideas about the nature of morality
that Kurt Baier expounded in The Moral Point of
View (1958). In effect, if not design, Gert’s theory
fully realized the program of recovering the
rational basis of ethics that Stephen Toulmin
and Baier advanced in opposition to the noncog-
nitivist accounts that dominated moral philoso-
phy in the 1940s and 1950s.
Gert was a leading expositor of Hobbes’s moral
philosophy. His interpretations show Hobbes to
be more sophisticated than he appears in stand-
ard treatments. In particular, Gert challenged the
standard treatment of Hobbes as an exponent of
psychological egoism and advanced an account
of the place of reason in Hobbes’s ethics on which
it is more than the engine of determinations of
means to ends. Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, Gert
earned his B.A. at the University of Cincinnati
and his Ph.D. at Cornell University, and taught
for ﬁfty years at Dartmouth College.
J.D.
Gesellschaft. See SOCIAL PHILOSOPHY.
Gestalt. See FIGURE-GROUND, KÖHLER.
Gestalt psychology. See KÖHLER.
Gettier problem. See EPISTEMOLOGY.
Gettier-style example. See EPISTEMOLOGY.
Geulincx, Arnold (1624–69), Dutch philoso-
pher born in Antwerp and educated at Louvain,
where he became professor of philosophy (1646)
and dean (1654). In 1657 he was forced out of
Louvain, perhaps for his Jansenist or Cartesian
tendencies, and in 1658 he moved to Leyden and
became a Protestant. Though he taught there
until his death, he never attained a regular pro-
fessorship at the university. His main philosoph-
ical work is his Ethica (1675), only Part I of which
appeared during his lifetime, as De Virtute et Primis
Ejus Proprietatibus (1665). Also published during
his lifetime were the Questiones Quodlibeticae
(1652; later editions published as Saturnalia),
the Logica (1661), and the Methodus Inveniendi
Argumenta (1665). His most important works,
though, were published posthumously; in addi-
tion to the Ethica, there is the Physica Vera (1688),
the Physica Peripatetica (1690), the Metaphysica
Vera (1691), and the Metaphysica ad Mentem
Peripateticam (1691). There are also two posthu-
mous commentaries on Descartes’s Principia
Philosophiae (1690 and 1691).
Geulincx was deeply inﬂuenced by Descartes,
and had many ideas that closely resemble those
of the later Cartesians as well as those of more
independent thinkers like Spinoza and Leibniz.
Though his grounds were original, like many
later Cartesians, Geulincx upheld a version of
occasionalism; he argued that someone or some-
thing can only do what it knows how to do,
inferring from that that we cannot be the genuine
causes of our own bodily movements. In discus-
sing the mind-body relation, Geulincx used
a clock analogy similar to one Leibniz used in
connection with his preestablished harmony.
Geulincx also held a view of mental and material
substance reminiscent of that of Spinoza. Finally,
he proposed a system of ethics grounded in the
idea of a virtuous will. Despite the evident sim-
ilarities between Geulincx’s views and the views
of his more renowned contemporaries, it is very
difﬁcult to determine exactly what inﬂuence
Geulincx may have had on them, and they may
have had on him.
See also DESCARTES, LEIBNIZ, OCCASIONALISM.

the self-cultivation process, subsequently given
different
interpretations
by

Confucian
thinkers. ‘Ge’ can mean ‘correct’, ‘arrive at’, or

mean ‘expand’ or ‘reach out’; the second ‘zhi’
means ‘knowledge’. Zhu Xi (1130–1200) took
‘gewu’ to mean arriving at li (principle, pattern)
in human affairs and ‘zhizhi’ to mean the expan-
sion of knowledge; an important part of the
self-cultivation
process
involves
expanding
one’s moral knowledge by examining daily
affairs and studying classics and historical docu-
ments. Wang Yangming (1472–1529) took ‘gewu’
to mean correcting the activities of one’s heart/
mind (xin), and ‘zhizhi’ the reaching out of one’s
innate knowledge (liangzhi); another important
part of the self-cultivation process involves
making fully manifest one’s innate knowledge

ghost in the machine. See RYLE.
Gibbard, Allan (b.1942), American philosopher
known for work in ethical theory, especially for
norm expressivism, developed in Wise Choices, Apt
Feelings (1990), Thinking How to Live (2003), and
Reconciling Our Aims (2008). On Gibbard’s view,
an act is morally wrong when it is rational for the
agent to feel guilty and for others to resent the
act, and to call something rational is to express
acceptance of norms that permit it. Expression
of norms one accepts is not assertion that one
accepts such norms, just as ‘Ugh!’ expresses
feelings and does not assert that one has those
feelings. Thus, this is noncognitivism concerning
rationality and morality. But like Blackburn,
Gibbard is a “quasi-realist” and hence aims to
explain much of the cognitivist appearance of
claims of rationality and morality. Acceptance of
norms, hypothesized to have evolved to aid coop-
eration, is acceptance of a plan of what to do in
actual and hypothetical circumstances. And such
plan-laden judgments have many logical and
semantic features of ordinary cognitive judg-
ments. In normative ethics, Gibbard is a utilitar-
ian on contractarian grounds, with afﬁnities to
John Harsanyi, Rawls, and Scanlon. In Meaning
and Normativity (2012), he applies norm expres-
sivism to linguistic meaning. In economics, he
is known for his work in social choice theory,
in particular the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem,
which states that any deterministic, non-dictatorial
voting system with more than two possible out-
comes is susceptible to strategic voting. In other
work, he defends contingent identity statements
between proper names and elaborates Ernest
Adams’s non-factualist view of indicative condi-
tionals and (with William Harper) Stalnaker’s
version of causal decision theory. He is Richard
B. Brandt Distinguished University Professor of
Philosophy at the University of Michigan.
A.Br. & J.Me.
Giles of Rome, original name, Egidio Colonna
(c.1243–1316), Italian theologian and ecclesias-
tic. A member of the order of the Hermits of
St. Augustine, he studied arts at an Augustinian
house and theology at the University in Paris
(1260–72) but was censured by the theology
faculty (1277) and denied a license to teach as
master. Owing to the intervention of Pope
Honorius IV, he later returned from Italy to
Paris to teach theology (1285–91), was appointed
general of his order (1292), and became arch-
bishop of Bourges (1295).
Giles both defended and criticized views of
Aquinas. He held that essence and existence
are really distinct in creatures, but described
them as “things”; that prime matter cannot
exist without some substantial form; and, early
in his career, that an eternally created world is
possible. He defended only one substantial form
in composites, including man. He supported
Pope Boniface VIII in his quarrel with Philip IV
of France.
J.F.W.
Gilson, Étienne (1884–1978), French Catholic
philosopher, historian, cofounder of the Pontiﬁcal
Institute of Medieval Studies in Toronto, and a
major ﬁgure in Neo-Thomism. Gilson discovered
medieval philosophy through his pioneering
work on Descartes’s Scholastic background. As a
historian, he argued that early modern philoso-
phy was incomprehensible without medieval
thought, and that medieval philosophy itself
did not represent the uniﬁed theory of reality
that some Thomists had supposed. His studies
of Duns Scotus, Augustine, Bernard, Aquinas,
Bonaventure, Dante, and Abelard and Héloïse
explore this diversity. But in his Gifford Lectures
(1931–32), The Spirit of Medieval Philosophy, Gilson
attempted a broad synthesis of medieval teaching
on philosophy, metaphysics, ethics, and episte-
mology, and employed it in his critique of
modern philosophy, The Unity of Philosophical
Experience (1937). Most of all, Gilson attempted
to reestablish Aquinas’s distinction between
essence and existence in created being, as in
Being and Some Philosophers (1949). See also
NEO-THOMISM, THOMISM.
D.W.H.
Gioberti, Vincenzo (1801–52), Italian philoso-
pher and statesman. He was an ordained priest,
was imprisoned and exiled for advocating Italian
uniﬁcation, and became a central political ﬁgure
during the Risorgimento. His major political
work, Del primato morale ecivile degli Italiani (“On
the Moral and Civil Primacy of Italians,” 1843),
argues for a federation of the Italian states with
the pope as its leader. Gioberti’s philosophical
theory, ontologism, in contrast to Hegel’s idealism,
identiﬁes the dialectics of Being with God’s
creation. He condensed his theory in the formula
“Being creates the existent.” The dialectics of
Being, which is the only necessary substance, is
a palingenesis, or a return to its origin, in which
the existent ﬁrst departs from and imitates its
417
Ghaza¯lı¯, al-
Gioberti, Vincenzo
creator (mimesis), and then returns to its creator
(methexis). By intuition, the human mind comes
in contact with God and discovers truth by retrac-
ing the dialectics of Being. However, knowledge
of supernatural truths is given only by God’s
revelation (Teorica del soprannaturale [“Theory
of the Supernatural,” 1838] and Introduzione
allo studio della ﬁlosoﬁa [“Introduction to the
Study of Philosophy,” 1841]). Gioberti criticized
modern philosophers such as Descartes for their
psychologism – seeking truth from the human
subject instead of from Being itself and its
revelation. His thought is still inﬂuential in Italy,
especially in Christian spiritualism.
P.Gar.
given, in epistemology, the “brute fact” element
found or postulated as a component of perceptual
experience. Some theorists who endorse the
existence of a given element in experience think
that we can ﬁnd this element by careful intro-
spection (Moore, H. H. Price). Such theorists
generally distinguish between those components
of ordinary perceptual awareness that constitute
what we believe or know about the objects we
perceive and those components that we strictly
perceive. For example, if we analyze introspec-
tively what we are aware of when we see an
apple, we ﬁnd that what we believe of the apple
is that it is a three-dimensional object with a soft,
white interior; what we see of it, strictly speaking,
is just a red expanse of its facing side. This latter is
what is “given” in the intended sense.
Other theorists treat the given as postulated
rather than introspectively found. For example,
some theorists treat cognition as imposing form
on some material given in conscious experience.
On this view, often attributed to Kant, the given
and the conceptual are interdeﬁned and logically
inseparable. Sometimes this interdependence is
seen as rendering a description of the given as
impossible; in this case the given is said to be
ineffable (C. I. Lewis, Mind and the World Order,
1929). On some theories of knowledge (founda-
tionalism) the ﬁrst variant of the given – that
which is “found” rather than “postulated” –
provides the empirical foundations of what we
might know or justiﬁably believe. Thus, if I believe
on good evidence that there is a red apple before
me, the evidence is the non-cognitive part of my
perceptual awareness of the red apple–shaped
expanse. Epistemologies postulating the ﬁrst kind
of givenness thus require a single entity-type
to explain the sensorial nature of perception
and to provide immediate epistemic foundations
for empirical knowledge. This requirement is
now widely regarded as impossible to satisfy;
hence Wilfrid Sellars describes the discredited
view as the myth of the given.
See also PERCEPTION; PHENOMENALISM; SELL-
ARS, WILFRID.
T.V.
given, myth of the. See SELLARS, WILFRID.
Glanvill, Joseph (1636–80), English philoso-
pher and Anglican minister who defended the
Royal Society against Scholasticism. Glanvill
believed that certainty was possible in mathe-
matics and theology, but not in empirical knowl-
edge. In his most important philosophical work,
The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), he claimed that
the human corruption that resulted from Adam’s
fall precludes dogmatic knowledge of nature.
Using traditional skeptical arguments as well as
an analysis of causality that partially anticipated
Hume, Glanvill argued that all empirical knowl-
edge is the probabilistic variety acquired by piece-
meal investigation. Despite his skepticism he
argued for the existence of witches in Witches
and Witchcraft (1668).
J.W.A.
Gleason’s theorem. See QUANTUM LOGIC.
global justice, principles governing the global
realm and focusing mainly on two concerns of
justice: substantial content (what is owed) and
scope (to whom it is owed). The former may be
limited by subjects, space, and time (intergenera-
tional justice). Global justice challenges the limits
set by subjects and space, and addresses the
relation between levels on which the principles
of justice may be applied: national (ius civitas),
transnational (ius cosmopoliticum), and interna-
tional (ius gentium). Political realism assumes
that states are concerned with pursuing self-
interest only, and any inequality in terms of
their power disqualiﬁes any concept of global
justice.
Global distributive justice concerns the fairness
of the distribution of resources beyond national
borders. For libertarianism, the just distribution
of goods can be guaranteed, both domestically
and globally, only by free exchange. There is,
however, disagreement regarding the appropri-
ate domain of distributive justice, the content of
the duties of justice, and the strength of duties of
justice toward compatriots and foreigners.
According to distributive statism, states are the
sole subjects determining the distribution of
goods, and principles of justice apply to a domes-
tic realm of institutions. Since there is no global
state, no global distribution of goods is justiﬁed
(with some exceptions, e.g. the redistribution of
418
given
global justice
natural resources and assistance in emergencies),
and global justice concerns the principles govern-
ing relations between internally just states.
According to distributive cosmopolitanism, free
and equal individuals are the primary subjects
of the distribution of goods; principles of justice
are applied to the global realm, and should not
be determined by nationality, which is an arbi-
trary condition. The requirements of justice are
equal in content and strength in the global and
domestic domains. One may distinguish between
institutional cosmopolitanism (principles of justice
applied to the global structure of cooperation)
and interactional cosmopolitanism (principles of jus-
tice applied to interactions between individuals).
Cosmopolitanism is challenged by national liber-
alism, which assumes a particularistic approach
to morality, claiming that national bonds produce
special moral obligations among compatriots
and that the principles of distributive justice are
justiﬁed only on the basis of shared values, i.e.
within a nation-state. The requirements of global
justice are different in content from those of
domestic justice, and produce weaker duties.
The alternative assumes a split-level conception
of distributive justice comprising principles of
distribution within and beyond national borders,
yet different in content in both domains, but
not necessarily different in strength.
See also COSMOPOLITANISM, ETHICS, JUSTICE,
KANT, POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY, SOCIAL PHILOSO-
PHY, UTILITARIANISM.
M.So.
global supervenience. See SUPERVENIENCE.
gnosticism, a dualistic religious and philosoph-
ical movement in the early centuries of the
Christian Church, especially important in the sec-
ond century under the leadership of Valentinus
and Basilides. They taught that matter was evil,
the result of a cosmic disruption in which an evil
archon (often associated with the God of the Old
Testament, Yahweh) rebelled against the heav-
enly pleroma (the complete spiritual world). In
the process divine sparks were unleashed from
the pleroma and lodged in material human
bodies. Jesus was a high-ranking archon (Logos)
sent to restore those souls with divine sparks to
the pleroma by imparting esoteric knowledge
(gnosis) to them.
Gnosticism inﬂuenced and threatened the
orthodox church from within and without.
Non-Christian gnostic sects rivaled Christianity,
and Christian gnostics threatened orthodoxy by
emphasizing salvation by knowledge rather than
by faith. Theologians like Clement of Alexandria
and his pupil Origen held that there were two
roads to salvation, the way of faith for the masses
and the way of esoteric or mystical knowledge for
the philosophers. Gnosticism profoundly inﬂu-
enced the early church, causing it to deﬁne its
scriptural canon and to develop a set of creeds
and an episcopal organization.
See also CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, ORIGEN.
L.P.P.

Göckel, Rudolph. See GOCLENIUS.
Goclenius, Rudolphus, in Germany, Rudolf
Göckel (1547–1628), German philosopher who
became professor at the University of Marburg
in 1581, where he remained until his death,
teaching physics, logic, mathematics, and ethics.
Though he was well read and knowledgeable of
later trends in these disciplines, his basic sympa-
thies were Aristotelian. Goclenius was highly
regarded by his contemporaries, who called him
the Plato of Marburg, the Christian Aristotle,
and the Light of Europe, among other things.
He published an unusually large number of
books, including the Psychologia, hoc est de hominis
perfectione. . . (1590), the Conciliator Philosophicus
(1609), the Controversiae Logicae et Philosophicae
(1609), and numerous other works on logic,
rhetoric, physics, metaphysics, and the Latin lan-
guage. His most lasting work was his Lexicon
Philosophicum (1613), together with its compan-
ion, the Lexicon Philosophicum Graecum (1615).
These lexicons provide clear deﬁnitions of the
philosophical terminology of late Scholastic phi-
losophy, and are still useful as reference works
for sixteenth- and early seventeenth-century
thought.
D.Garb.

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, two theo-
rems formulated and proved by the Austrian
logician Kurt Gödel (1906–78) in his famous
419
global supervenience
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
1931 paper “Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze
der
Principia
Mathematica
und
vervandter
Systeme I,” probably the most celebrated results
in the whole of logic. They are aptly referred to
as “incompleteness” theorems since each shows,
for any member of a certain class of formal
systems, that there is a sentence formulable in
its language that it cannot prove, but that it
would be desirable for it to prove. In the case of
the ﬁrst theorem (G1), what cannot be proved is a
true sentence of the language of the given theory.
G1 is thus a disappointment to theory construc-
tors who want their theory to tell the whole truth
about its subject. In the case of the second theo-
rem (G2), what cannot be proved is a sentence
of the theory that “expresses” its consistency. G2
is thus a disappointment to those who desire a
straightforward execution of Hilbert’s Program.
The proofs of the incompleteness theorems
can be seen as based on three main ideas. The
ﬁrst is that of a Gödel numbering – i.e., an assign-
ment of natural numbers to each of the various
objects (i.e., the terms, formulas, axioms, proofs,
etc.) belonging to the various syntactical catego-
ries of the given formal system T (referred to here
as the “represented theory”) whose metamathe-
matics is under consideration. The second is
that of a representational scheme. This includes
(i) the use of the Gödel numbering to develop
number-theoretic codiﬁcations of various of the
metamathematical properties pertaining to the
represented theory, and (ii) the selection of a
theory S (hereafter, the “representing theory”)
and a family of formulas from that theory (the
“representing formulas”) in terms of which to
register as theorems various of the facts concern-
ing the metamathematical properties of the rep-
resented theory thus encoded. The basic result
of this representational scheme is the weak
representation of the set of (Gödel numbers of)
theorems of T, where a set Λ of numbers is said
to be weakly represented in S by a formula ‘L(x)’
of S just in case for every number v, v ∈Λ if and
only if ‘L([v])’ is a theorem of S, where ‘[v]’ is
the standard term of S that, under the intended
interpretation of S, designates the number n.
Since the set of (Gödel numbers of) theorems of
the represented theory T will typically be recur-
sively enumerable, and the representing theory
S must be capable of weakly representing this
set, the basic strength requirement on S is that it
be capable of weakly representing the recursively
enumerable sets of natural numbers. Because
basic systems of arithmetic (e.g., Robinson’s
arithmetic and Peano arithmetic) all have this
capacity, Gödel’s theorems are often stated
using containment of a fragment of arithmetic
as the basic strength requirement governing the
capacities of the representing theory (which, of
course, is also often the represented theory).
More on this point below.
The third main idea behind the incompleteness
theorems is that of a diagonal or ﬁxed point con-
struction within S for the notion of unprovability-
in-T – i.e., the formulation of a sentence Gödel of S
which, under the given Gödel numbering of T,
the given representation of T’s metamathemati-
cal notions in S, and the intended interpretation
of the language of S, says of itself that it is not
provable-in-T. Gödel is thus false if provable and
unprovable if true. More speciﬁcally, if ‘ProvT(x)’
is a formula of S that weakly represents the set of
(Gödel numbers of) theorems of T in S, then Gödel
can be any formula of S that is provably equiv-
alent in S to the formula ‘~ProvT ([Gödel])’.
Given this background, G1 can be stated as
follows: If (a) the representing theory S is any
subtheory of the represented theory T (up to and
including the represented theory itself), (b) the
representing theory S is consistent, (c) the
formula ‘ProvT(x)’ weakly represents the set of
(Gödel numbers of) theorems of the represented
theory T in the representing theory S, and
(d) Gödel is any sentence provably equivalent in
the representing theory S to ‘ProvT ([Gödel])’, then
neither Gödel nor ~Gödel is a theorem of the rep-
resenting theory S.
The proof proceeds in two parts. In the ﬁrst part
it is shown that, for any representing theory S (up
to and including the case where S = T), if S is
consistent, then ~Gödel is not a theorem of S.
To obtain this in its strongest form, we pick the
strongest subtheory S of T possible, namely S = T,
and construct a reductio. Thus, suppose that
(1) ~Gödel is a theorem of T. From (1) and (d) it
follows that (2) ‘ProvT([Gödel])’ is a theorem of T.
And from (2) and (c) (in the “if” direction) it
follows that (3) Gödel is a theorem of T. But (1)
and (3) together imply that the representing
theory T is inconsistent. Hence, if T is consistent,
~Gödel cannot be a theorem of T.
In the second part of the proof it is argued that
if the representing theory S is consistent, then
Gödel is not a theorem of it. Again, to obtain
the strongest result, we let S be the strongest
subtheory of T possible (namely T itself) and, as
before, argue by reductio. Thus we suppose that
(A) Gödel is a theorem of S (= T ). From this
assumption and condition (d) it follows that
(B) ‘~Prov([Gödel])’ is a theorem of S (= T ). By
(A) and (c) (in the “only if” direction) it follows
that (C) ‘ProvT ([Gödel])’ is a theorem of S (= T ).
420
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
But from (B) and (C) it follows that S (= T ) is
inconsistent. Hence, Gödel is not provable in any
consistent representing theory S up to and
including T itself.
The above statement of G1 is, of course, not the
usual one. The usual statement suppresses the
distinction stressed above between the represent-
ing and represented theories and collaterally
replaces our condition (c) with a clause to the
effect that T is a recursively axiomatizable exten-
sion of some suitably weak system of arithmetic
(e.g., Robinson’s arithmetic, primitive recursive
arithmetic, or Peano arithmetic). This puts into a
single clause what, metamathematically speak-
ing, are two separate conditions – one pertaining
to the representing theory, the other to the
represented theory. The requirement that T be
an extension of the selected weak arithmetic
addresses the question of T’s adequacy as a rep-
resenting theory, since the crucial fact about
extensions of the weak arithmetic chosen is that
they are capable of weakly representing all recur-
sively enumerable sets. This constraint on T’s
capabilities as a representing theory is in partner-
ship with the usual requirement that, in its
capacity as a represented theory, T be recursively
axiomatizable. For T’s recursive axiomatizability
ensures (under ordinary choices of logic for T)
that its set of theorems will be recursively enu-
merable – and hence weakly representable in the
kind of representing theory that it itself (by virtue
of its being an extension of the weak arithmetic
speciﬁed) is.
G1 can, however, be extended to certain theo-
ries whose sets of (Gödel numbers of) theorems
are not recursively enumerable. When this is
done, the basic capacity required of the repre-
senting theory is no longer merely that the recur-
sively enumerable sets of natural numbers be
representable in it, but that it also be capable of
representing various non-recursively enumera-
ble sets, and hence that it go beyond the weak
arithmetics mentioned earlier.
G2 is a more demanding result than G1 in that
it puts signiﬁcantly stronger demands on the
formula ‘ProvT(x)’ used to express the notion
of provability for the represented theory T. In
proving G1 all that is required of ‘ProvT(x)’ is
that it weakly represent θ (= the set of Gödel
numbers of theorems of T ) – i.e., that it yield an
extensionally accurate registry of the theorems
of the represented theory in the representing
theory.
G2
places
additional
conditions
on
‘ProvT(x)’, conditions which result from the fact
that, to prove G2, we must codify the second part
of the proof of G1 in T itself. To do this, ‘ProvT(x)’
must be a provability predicate for T. That is, it
must satisfy the following constraints, commonly
referred to as the derivability conditions (for
‘ProvT(x)’):
(I) If A is a theorem of the represented
theory, then ‘ProvT ([A])’ must be a theo-
rem of the representing theory.
(II) Every instance of the formula ‘ProvT([A →
B]) →(ProvT([A]) →ProvT([B]))’ must be
a theorem of T.
(III) Every instance of the formula ‘ProvT([A])
→ProvT([ProvT([A])])’ must be a theo-
rem of T.
(I), of course, is just part of the requirement that
‘ProvT([A])’ weakly represent T’s theorem-set in
T. So it does not go beyond what is required for
the proof of G1. (II) and (III), however, do. They
make it possible to “formalize” the second part of
the proof of G1 in T itself. (II) captures, in terms of
‘ProvT(X)’, the modus ponens inference by which
(B) is derived from (A), and (III) codiﬁes in T the
appeal to (c) used in deriving (C) from (A).
The result of this “formalization” process is
a proof within T of the formula ‘ConT →Gödel’
(where
ConT
is
a
formula
of
the
form
‘~ ProvT([#])’, with ‘ProvT(x)’ a provability pred-
icate for T and ‘[#]’ the standard numeral denot-
ing the Gödel number # of some formula
refutable in T). From this, and the proof of
the second part of G1 itself (in which the ﬁrst
derivability condition, which is just the “only if”
direction of (c), ﬁgures prominently), we arrive at
the following result, which is a generalized form
of G2: if S is any consistent representing theory
up to and including the represented theory
T itself, ‘ProvT(x)’ any provability predicate for
T, and ConT any formula of T of the form
‘~ ProvT([#])’, then ConT is not a theorem of S.
To the extent that, in being a provability predicate
for T, ‘ProvT(x)’ “expresses” the notion of prov-
ability of the represented theory T, it seems fair
to say that ConT expresses its consistency. And
to the extent that this is true, it is sensible to read
G2 as saying that for any representing theory S
and any represented theory T extending S, if S is
consistent, then the consistency of T is not prov-
able in S.
See also

THEORY,
CONSISTENCY,

Godfrey of Fontaines (probably before 1250–
1306 or 1309), French philosopher. He taught
theology at Paris (1285–c.1299; 1303–1304).
Among his major writings are ﬁfteen Quodlibetal
Questions and other disputations. He was strongly
421
Godfrey of Fontaines
Godfrey of Fontaines
Aristotelian
in
philosophy,
with
Neoplatonic
inﬂuences in metaphysics. He defended the iden-
tity of essence and existence in creatures against
theories of their real or intentional distinction, and
argued for the possibility of demonstrating God’s
existence and of some quidditative knowledge of
God. He admitted divine ideas for species but
not for individuals within species. He made wide
applications of Aristotelian act-potency theory –
e.g., to the distinction between the soul and its
powers, to the explanation of intellection and
volition, to the general theory of substance and
accident, and in unusual fashion to essence-
existence “composition” of creatures.
J.F.W.
Godwin, William (1756–1836), English philos-
opher, novelist, and political writer. Godwin’s
main philosophical treatise, Enquiry concerning
Political Justice (1793), aroused heated debate.
He argued for radical forms of determinism, anar-
chism, and utilitarianism. Government corrupts
everyone by encouraging stereotyped thinking
that prevents us from seeing each other as unique
individuals. Godwin’s novel Caleb Williams (1794)
portrays a good man corrupted by prejudice. Once
we remove prejudice and artiﬁcial inequality
we will see that our acts are wholly determined.
This makes punishment pointless. Only in small,
anarchic societies can people see others as they
really are and thus come to feel sympathetic con-
cern for their well-being. Only so can we be virtu-
ous, because virtue is acting from sympathetic
feelings to bring the greatest happiness to all
affected.
Godwin took this principle quite literally, and
accepted all its consequences. Truthfulness has
no claim on us other than the happiness it brings.
If keeping a promise causes less good than break-
ing it, there is no reason at all to keep it. If one
must choose between saving the life either of a
major human benefactor or of one’s mother, one
must choose the benefactor. Ideally we would
need no rules in morals at all. They prevent us
from seeing others properly, thereby impairing
the sympathetic feelings that constitute virtue.
Rights are pointless since sympathetic people
will act to help others. Later utilitarians like
Bentham had difﬁculty in separating their posi-
tions from Godwin’s notorious views.
See also BENTHAM.
J.B.S.
Goethe, Johann Wolfgang von (1749–1832),
German writer often considered the leading
cultural ﬁgure of his age. His career spans as
well as transcends the literary period of Sturm
and Drang (storm and stress), neo-classicism,
and romanticism. He wrote lyric poetry, dramas,
and ﬁctional, essayistic, and aphoristic prose
as well as works in various natural sciences,
including anatomy, botany, and optics. A lawyer
by training, for most of his life Goethe was a
government ofﬁcial at the provincial court of
Saxony-Weimar. In his numerous contributions
to world literature, such as the novels The Sorrows
of Young Werther (1774), Wilhelm Meister’s Years of
Apprenticeship (1795/96), Elective Afﬁnities (1809),
and Wilhelm Meister’s Years of Pilgrimage (1821/29),
and
the
two-part
tragedy
Faust
(1808/32),
Goethe represented the tensions between indi-
vidual and society as well as between culture and
nature, with increased recognition of their tragic
opposition and the need to cultivate a resigned
self-discipline in artistic and social matters. In
his poetic and scientiﬁc treatment of nature he
was inﬂuenced by Spinoza’s pantheist identiﬁca-
tion of nature and God and maintained that
everything in nature is animate and expressive
of divine presence. In his theory and practice of
science he opposed the quantitative and exper-
imental method and insisted on a description of
the phenomena that was to include the intuitive
grasp of the archetypal forms or shapes under-
lying all development in nature. See also
GERMAN PHILOSOPHY, PANTHEISM, SPINOZA. G.Z.
